title: The oldest known art
description: The oldest reliably dated cave art is a hand stencil on Muna island, Indonesia, at least 67,800 years old; art is far older than writing.

facts.text: A hand stencil in Liang Metanduno cave on Muna island, Indonesia, is at least 67,800 years old, the oldest reliably dated cave art yet found.
A hand stencil is made by pressing a hand to the rock and blowing or spraying pigment such as red ochre over it, so the hand's outline stays on bare rock.
Writing (Sumerian cuneiform) emerged around the end of the 4th millennium BCE, about 5,200 years ago.
Leonardo da Vinci began painting the Mona Lisa about 1503.

Squeezing the 67,800 years since the oldest known cave art into one 24-hour day, writing (about 5,200 years ago) appears just after 10 p.m., after more than 22 hours, and the Mona Lisa (about 1503) about 11 minutes before midnight.

title: The big eras of art
description: Western art history is told as a run of eras (Stone Age, ancient, medieval, Renaissance, Baroque, modern), each partly answering the one before.

facts.text: Britannica's history of Western painting runs from the Stone Age through ancient Greece and Rome, the Middle Ages, the Renaissance, the Baroque and the Neoclassical and Romantic periods to modern art.
Prehistoric art includes paintings on cave walls, like those at Chauvet and Lascaux, and small portable carvings in bone and ivory.
Ancient Egyptian art, made over about three thousand years BCE, served the king and the gods.
From late antiquity to the Counter-Reformation, Western art was essentially the art of the church.
Renaissance is French for 'rebirth'; beginning in 14th-century Italy, it revived the learning and art of ancient Greece and Rome.
Baroque art, roughly of the 1600s, aimed for drama, movement and emotion.
Modern painting began in mid-19th-century France and rejected traditional rules; photography freed painting from being the only way to depict the world accurately.

title: Bird in Space on trial
description: In 1926 US customs taxed Brancusi's Bird in Space as metal because it did not look like a bird; in 1928 a court ruled it a work of art.

facts.text: In 1926 US customs refused to accept Constantin Brancusi's bronze Bird in Space as a sculpture and charged a 40% duty on it as a manufacture of metal.
In Bird in Space, Brancusi left out wings and feathers, elongated the body and reduced the head and beak to a slanted oval; the bronze is polished like a mirror.
Bird in Space conveys the idea of flight rather than the look of a particular bird.
In 1928 a US customs court ruled Bird in Space an original sculpture and a work of art, recognizing a new school of art that portrays abstract ideas rather than imitating natural objects.
The court admitted it might be hard to associate the sculpture with a bird, but found it pleasing to look at.

title: What counts as art?
description: People have disagreed over whether art must imitate nature or may express ideas; the Brancusi case shows the old and new definitions colliding.

facts.text: Before the Brancusi case, US courts treated sculpture as work carved or shaped in the likeness of natural models, such as people and animals.
At the trial, critic Frank Crowninshield testified that the work suggested flight, grace and speed, just as a bird does.

title: The elements of art
description: The building blocks of any artwork: line, shape, color, texture and space (many lists add form).

facts.text: The elements of art are the building blocks artists use to make a work of art: line, shape, form, space, color and texture.
A line is a mark longer than it is wide; lines can be straight or curved, thick or thin.
A shape is a closed line; shapes are flat and can be geometric, like squares and circles, or organic, like free-form natural shapes.
In art, color is light reflected off objects.
Texture is the surface quality of a work, real or implied; a drawing of a porcupine may look prickly, but the paper is still smooth.
Form means three-dimensional shapes, such as balls, cylinders and boxes.

title: Space and negative space
description: Space is the area around and between things; the empty part, negative space, has a shape too. Space also means the feeling of depth.

facts.text: Space is the area around and between objects; the empty space around them is negative space, which has a shape too. Space can also mean the feeling of depth.

title: The color wheel and primary colors
description: Newton bent the spectrum into a circle; painters' primaries are red, yellow and blue, and mixing two gives a secondary color.

facts.text: In Opticks (1704), Isaac Newton arranged the colors of the spectrum in a circle, an early color wheel.
In traditional color theory for painters, the primary colors are red, yellow and blue; other colors are mixes of them.
Mixing two primary colors makes a secondary color: orange, green or violet.

title: Complementary colors
description: Complements sit opposite on the color wheel; side by side they make each other look more intense (Chevreul's simultaneous contrast), mixed they make brown.

facts.text: Complementary colors sit directly across the color wheel, such as red and green, blue and orange, and yellow and violet; each pair shares no common primary.
Mixed together, complementary paints neutralize each other and make brown.
Soon after becoming director of dyeing at the Gobelins royal tapestry works in Paris in 1824, chemist Michel-Eugène Chevreul received complaints that the tapestry colors looked weak.
Chevreul found the problem was optical, not the dye: colors placed side by side change how each other look. He published this law of simultaneous contrast in 1839.
Complementary colors placed side by side make each other look more intense.
Chevreul's color ideas influenced painters, including the Impressionists.

title: The oldest known drawing
description: A crosshatch drawn in red ochre on a stone flake at Blombos Cave, South Africa, about 73,000 years old; whether it is art is debated.

facts.text: A crosshatch drawn with a red ochre crayon on a stone flake from Blombos Cave, South Africa, is about 73,000 years old, the oldest known drawing.
The Blombos drawing is at least 30,000 years older than other known abstract and figurative drawings.
Researchers debate whether the Blombos lines were meant as art; they may instead be left over from sharpening the ochre crayon.
Cave artists made reds from iron oxides such as hematite (red ochre) and blacks from manganese dioxide and charcoal.

title: Hand stencils
description: How hand stencils were made by blowing pigment around a hand, and how the Muna stencil's fingers were narrowed into a claw.

facts.text: Someone later narrowed the fingers of the Muna hand stencil, making it look like a claw.
Cave artists sometimes blew pigment onto the wall through a pipe.

title: The oldest picture story
description: A scene of three human-like figures and a wild pig at Leang Karampuang, Sulawesi, at least 51,200 years old, dated from mineral crusts over the paint.

facts.text: A cave painting at Leang Karampuang, Sulawesi, showing three human-like figures interacting with a wild pig, is at least 51,200 years old, the oldest known narrative art.
The Leang Karampuang scene was dated by uranium-series analysis of thin calcium carbonate crusts that formed on top of the paint.

title: Lascaux
description: The Lascaux cave paintings in France: found in 1940, about 17,000 years old, the Hall of the Bulls, and closed in 1963 after visitors damaged them.

facts.text: Lascaux cave in France was discovered by four teenagers in September 1940.
Radiocarbon dating of charcoal from Lascaux gives a date of about 17,000 years ago.
Lascaux's Hall of the Bulls holds four huge black bulls, or aurochs, some about 5 meters long, with their horns shown in 'twisted perspective'.
Lascaux's painters used scaffolding to reach high walls and the ceiling.
Lascaux opened to the public in 1948; up to 100,000 visitors a year and artificial lighting faded its colors and brought algae, bacteria and crystals, so it closed in 1963.
A partial replica, Lascaux II, opened nearby in 1983.
Lascaux's paintings lasted about 17,000 years in the dark, then about 15 years of public visits (1948 to 1963) damaged them.

title: Chauvet
description: Chauvet Cave in France: about 35,500 years old, full of dangerous animals, drawn with scraped walls, strong outlines and shading.

facts.text: In 1994, explorers found Chauvet Cave in southern France after feeling a faint draft from a heap of stones.
Rockfalls blocked Chauvet Cave's entrance, and the last one sealed it at least 21,000 years ago, until explorers found it in 1994.
Radiocarbon dating of charcoal and drawings shows most of Chauvet's art is about 35,500 years old, roughly twice Lascaux's age.
Chauvet holds over 400 images of animals from 14 species, with many dangerous ones: cave lions, woolly rhinos, mammoths and bears.
Chauvet's artists scraped walls to make a blank surface, strengthened outlines to make figures stand out and used stump drawing (smudging) for shading.
In Chauvet's End Chamber, lions are shown hunting bison.

title: The Lion-Man
description: A mammoth-ivory figure with a lion's head and upright human body, about 40,000 years old, from Hohlenstein-Stadel cave in Germany.

facts.text: The Lion-Man, carved from mammoth ivory about 40,000 years ago, has a cave lion's head on an upright, partly human body.
The Lion-Man was found in Hohlenstein-Stadel cave in Germany; it is 31 cm tall, the largest known sculpture of Ice Age art.
Carving a copy of the Lion-Man with Ice Age-style stone tools took an experimenter hundreds of hours.

title: Ice Age figures of women
description: Small Ice Age carvings of women such as the Venus of Hohle Fels and the Venus of Willendorf, and why their meaning and name are uncertain.

facts.text: The Venus of Hohle Fels, from a German cave, is a 6 cm mammoth-ivory figure of a woman, 35,000 to 40,000 years old, with a pierced loop instead of a head, so it may have been worn as a pendant.
The Venus of Willendorf, found in Austria in 1908, is an 11.1 cm limestone figure of a woman tinted with red ochre, about 30,000 years old, with no face, only a pattern like a braid or cap.
The name 'Venus', after the Roman goddess of love, was given by modern scholars; the figures were carved many thousands of years before Rome.
Ideas about the Venus of Willendorf include a fertility figure, a good-luck charm and a mother goddess.
A 2022 study found the Venus of Willendorf's stone likely came from the Lake Garda region of northern Italy, across the Alps.

title: Stonehenge
description: How Stonehenge was built: dates, where the stones came from, the woodworking joints and the hundreds of people needed.

facts.text: Stonehenge began as a circular ditch and bank about 3000 BC; its stones were set up about 2500 BC, roughly 4,500 years ago.
Stonehenge's sarsens, about 25 tons on average, came from West Woods about 25 km away; its bluestones came from the Preseli Hills in Wales, more than 200 km away.
Stonehenge's lintels were fitted with mortise-and-tenon and tongue-and-groove joints, usually found only in woodworking.
Building the stone circle needed hundreds of people to move, shape and raise the stones.

title: Gatherings at Stonehenge
description: Stonehenge's solstice alignment and the midwinter feasts at Durrington Walls, with animals brought from across Britain.

facts.text: Stonehenge is aligned with the Sun: at midsummer the sun rises beside the Heel Stone, and at midwinter it originally set between the uprights of the tallest trilithon.

At Durrington Walls near Stonehenge, over 38,000 animal bones have been found; pig teeth show animals raised as far away as west Wales, northern England and north-east Scotland, slaughtered at midwinter for feasts.

title: Göbekli Tepe
description: Carved T-shaped stone pillars built by hunter-gatherers about 11,500 years ago, before farming.

facts.text: Göbekli Tepe in southeastern Turkey was built by hunter-gatherers, before farming, beginning about 11,500 years ago: more than twice Stonehenge's age.
Göbekli Tepe's T-shaped limestone pillars reach over 5 meters tall and weigh up to 50 tons; some are carved with foxes, scorpions and lions.
Some Göbekli Tepe pillars have carved arms and hands meeting across the front, and belts; researchers read the T-pillars as larger-than-life stylized people.
Göbekli Tepe suggests that building together may have led people to settle, rather than following settlement.

title: Art to record the world
description: Ideas that early art came from a basic urge to record the world, or served as records such as counts and seasonal calendars.

facts.text: The exact purpose of prehistoric art is still debated.
One view sees Paleolithic art as coming from a basic human need to creatively record and recreate the world around us.
Some researchers suggest Paleolithic animal images showing seasonal coats may be an early seasonal notation system.
Researchers suggest the patterns on an engraved ochre plaque from Blombos Cave may be a way of counting or storing information.

title: The hunting magic idea
description: The idea that animal images were magic for successful hunts, and the Lascaux reindeer problem.

facts.text: Some scholars see prehistoric animal images as magic to make hunting succeed or to guarantee fertility.
Reindeer were the Lascaux artists' main food, yet reindeer are almost absent from Lascaux's walls.

title: The spirit world idea
description: The idea that cave art was symbolic or religious, perhaps tied to shamans and part-human, part-animal beings.

facts.text: Cave art is generally thought to have had a symbolic or religious function, sometimes both.
Some experts think cave art was made within shamanic beliefs, in which a shaman enters a trance to contact spirits.
Researchers suggest the Muna stencil's claw-like fingers may reflect links between people and animals, or spiritual beliefs.

title: How cave art is dated
description: Radiocarbon dates once-living material like charcoal; uranium-series dates mineral crusts over paint, giving a minimum age.

facts.text: Radiocarbon dating measures carbon-14 in once-living material such as charcoal, and works for specimens up to about 50,000 years old.
Many cave paintings use mineral pigments with no organic material, so radiocarbon cannot date them.
Uranium-series dating of mineral crusts that formed on top of a painting gives a minimum age: the paint underneath must be older.

title: Ziggurats
description: Mesopotamian cities built stepped temple towers of mud brick, like the ziggurat of Ur, with a temple on top.

facts.text: Mesopotamia, Greek for 'between rivers', is the land of the Tigris and Euphrates, where the world's earliest civilization developed.
A ziggurat was a stepped temple tower of the major cities of ancient Mesopotamia, built with a core of mud brick and an outer skin of baked brick.
The ziggurat at Ur was built about 2100 BCE under King Ur-Nammu for the moon god Nanna; it had three staircases and a temple on its flat top.

title: Cylinder seals
description: Mesopotamians carved small stone cylinders that printed a continuous picture when rolled on wet clay, used like a signature.

facts.text: A cylinder seal is a small stone cylinder carved into its surface; rolled across wet clay, it leaves a continuous raised impression of the design.
Cylinder seals were often no bigger than 5 cm tall, carved from stones such as lapis lazuli, agate or limestone.
Cylinder seals are counted among ancient Mesopotamia's finest artistic achievements.
Cylinder seals marked personal property and made documents legally binding; rolled on a clay tablet, a seal showed its owner authorized the text, like a signature.
Sumerian cuneiform was written by pressing the slanted edge of a stylus into soft clay tablets, making wedge-shaped marks.

title: The composite view
description: Egyptian artists drew each body part from its most complete angle: head in profile, eye and shoulders frontal, legs in profile.

facts.text: Egyptian artists drew a figure with the head in profile, the eye as if seen from the front, the shoulders frontal and the legs in profile.
Egyptian artists combined viewpoints to show each part of the body in its most complete, most recognizable form.

title: Egypt's rules: grid and scale
description: A shared 18-unit grid and size-shows-importance kept Egyptian art consistent for about 3,000 years.

facts.text: Egyptian art kept its general character for about 3,000 years, though it did change over time.
For most of Egyptian history, a standing figure measured 18 equal units from the soles of the feet to the hairline, laid out on a grid; crowns varied, so the top of the head was left out.
In Egyptian art, size showed importance: kings dwarf officials, and tomb owners dwarf their families and servants.

title: Art for the ka
description: Egyptians filled tombs with pictures and models of food and daily life so the ka, the life force, would be fed forever.

facts.text: The ka, a person's life force, still needed food and drink after death, so tombs held scenes and models of food that could feed it forever without being used up.
Egyptians hoped the afterlife would continue their daily lives on Earth without pain, and tomb art showed the dead as they wished to remain forever.
As the focus of offerings, an Egyptian tomb was known as the ka house.

title: Tomb models and shabtis
description: Figures like Meketre's models and shabtis were buried to provide for and work for the dead in the afterlife.

facts.text: In 1920, Metropolitan Museum excavators found a small hidden chamber in the long-robbed tomb of the official Meketre, sealed almost 4,000 years, holding 24 painted wooden models.
Meketre's models show boats, offering bearers, and buildings with craftsmen and people preparing food such as bread and beer.
Egyptians believed images could magically give the dead safe passage to the afterlife and eternal food there.
Shabtis were small figures buried in tombs as substitute workers, to do the dead person's labor in the afterlife.

title: Black-figure vases
description: Greek painters put figures in black on the red clay and scratched details through the black.

facts.text: Exekias signed an amphora of 540–530 BCE, now in the Vatican Museums, as potter and painter; it shows Achilles and Ajax seated, playing a dice game.
On Exekias's amphora, inscriptions come from the heroes' mouths like a comic strip: Achilles calls four and Ajax calls three.
In black-figure vase painting, figures were painted in glossy black on the natural clay, and details were scratched (incised) through the black.
Black-figure painting arose in Corinth about 700 BCE, and Athenian potters took it up at the end of the 7th century BCE.
The black on Greek vases is a fine clay slip that turns glossy black in a three-stage firing that switches the kiln between oxidizing and reducing; the bare clay returns to orange-red.

title: Red-figure vases
description: About 530 BCE Athenian painters reversed black-figure: black background, red figures, details painted with a brush.

facts.text: Red-figure painting, invented in Athens about 530 BCE, reversed black-figure: the background was painted black and the figures left in red clay, with details painted rather than incised.
Painted details gave red-figure artists more freedom to show the human body, movement and facial expressions, and red-figure became the dominant style.

title: The kouros
description: Archaic Greek statues of young men stood stiff and frontal, left foot forward, in a pose that reflects Egyptian traditions.

facts.text: A kouros is an Archaic Greek statue of a standing young man; large stone kouroi appeared about 615–590 BCE and stayed popular until about 460 BCE, some as grave markers.
Early kouroi are stiffly frontal, with the left foot slightly forward and the arms close to the body, fists clenched.
The kouros reflects Egyptian traditions, especially Egyptian systems of body proportion.

title: Contrapposto
description: Greek sculptors learned to rest a figure's weight on one leg, tilting hips and shoulders so the statue looks alive.

facts.text: Contrapposto puts a figure's weight on one leg with the other bent, so the hips, shoulders and head tilt; the Greeks developed it in the early 5th century BCE to replace stiff poses.
The marble Kritios Boy, from the Athenian Acropolis, dates to just after 480 BCE; he rests his weight on his left leg, the right leg relaxed and bent at the knee.
Polyclitus made the Doryphoros (Spear Bearer), about 450–440 BCE, to illustrate his book the Canon on the ideal proportions of the human body.
Polyclitus's use of contrapposto helped free Greek sculpture from rigid, face-front poses.

title: The three Greek orders
description: Greek columns come in three styles: plain Doric, scrolled Ionic and leafy Corinthian.

facts.text: Classical Greek architecture has three orders, or column styles: Doric, Ionic and Corinthian.
Greek Doric columns have no base and a plain, cushion-like capital; they are the sturdiest-looking order.
Ionic capitals have scrolls (volutes), and Ionic columns stand on a base and are more slender.
Corinthian capitals are carved with rows of acanthus leaves; it is the most decorative order.
The Romans adopted the Doric, Ionic and Corinthian orders and modified them.

title: The Parthenon
description: Athena's marble temple in Athens, the high point of the Doric order, built with subtle curves whose purpose is still debated.

facts.text: The Parthenon, a white marble temple for the goddess Athena, was begun in 447 BCE and completed by 438 BCE, with decoration continuing until 432 BCE.
The Parthenon is the culmination of the Doric order, the simplest of the three; its architects were Ictinus and Callicrates, under the sculptor Phidias.
The Parthenon's base curves upward, about 5 cm higher in the middle, its columns bulge slightly (entasis), and its corner columns are thicker.
The Roman architect Vitruvius explained such curves as corrections for optical illusions; a 2026 study by mathematician Alain Goriely argues there is no evidence they produce those illusions.

title: Rome copies Greece
description: Romans admired Greek art and copied it; some Greek masterpieces survive only as Roman copies.

facts.text: None of Polyclitus's original works survive; the Doryphoros is known only through Roman copies.
In the last century of the Roman Republic, admiration for earlier Greek art came into fashion in Rome.

title: Verism: warts and all
description: Roman portrait busts recorded every wrinkle, because an aged face signaled dignity and authority.

facts.text: In Roman realistic portraiture, every line, crease, wrinkle and even blemish was recorded.
Realistic portraiture appeared in Rome as a sudden flowering around 100 BCE.
In veristic portraits, the wrinkles of age, particularly in men, were signs of dignity and authority, symbols of experience.

title: The Pantheon's dome
description: Hadrian's Pantheon spans about 43 m in unreinforced concrete, lit by one opening, the oculus.

facts.text: The emperor Hadrian rebuilt the Pantheon in Rome between 118 and 128 CE: a round building of brick-faced concrete under a great concrete dome.
The Pantheon's dome is about 43 m across and is lit only by an opening about 8 m wide at its top, the oculus.
The Pantheon's dome is unreinforced concrete, with no steel inside, and was unmatched in scale until modern times.

title: How mosaics are made
description: Mosaics are pictures built from small closely set pieces called tesserae; Romans laid them on floors across the empire.

facts.text: At the entrance of Pompeii's House of the Tragic Poet, a floor mosaic shows a black dog on a chain with the words CAVE CANEM, 'Beware of the dog'; Vesuvius buried Pompeii in 79 CE.
A mosaic is a design made of closely set small pieces of stone, glass, tile or shell, called tesserae, from Latin for 'cubes' or 'dice'.
The Greeks refined pebble mosaics and then invented cut tesserae, shaped to fit closely together, which allowed denser, more detailed pictures.
Roman mosaics spread throughout the empire as floor decoration.

title: The Alexander Mosaic
description: A Pompeii floor of about 100 BCE, made of more than a million tesserae, showing Alexander fighting Darius, likely a copy of a lost Greek painting.

facts.text: The Alexander Mosaic, from the House of the Faun in Pompeii, dates to about 100 BCE, is about 5.8 m wide and is made of more than a million tesserae.
The Alexander Mosaic shows Alexander the Great fighting the Persian king Darius III at the Battle of Issus.
Scholars believe the Alexander Mosaic is a Roman copy of a lost Greek painting.

title: The Terracotta Army
description: About 8,000 life-size clay soldiers, each with its own face, guard the tomb of China's first emperor.

facts.text: The Terracotta Army was found in March 1974, when farmers drilling a well broke into an underground chamber.
About 8,000 life-size terra-cotta figures were buried to guard the tomb of Qin Shi Huang, first emperor of a unified China, who died in 210 BCE.
The soldiers were assembled from separately fired sections but each was given an individually detailed face.
The army's weapons, cast from an unusual metal alloy, are still shiny and sharp today.

title: Showing the Buddha
description: Early Buddhist art showed the Buddha only through symbols; around the 1st century CE Gandhara and Mathura began showing him in human form.

facts.text: On the gateways of Sanchi's Great Stupa in India, added in the 1st century BCE, carved stories of the Buddha's life show him only as a wheel, an empty throne or a pair of footprints.
Around the 1st century CE, sculptors at Gandhara and at Mathura each independently began showing the Buddha in human form.
Gandhara, in today's northwestern Pakistan and eastern Afghanistan, gave the Buddha a youthful, Apollo-like face and robes like those on Roman imperial statues.

title: The lost colors of ancient art
description: Greek and Roman statues and the Terracotta Army were brightly painted; most of the color has since been lost.

facts.text: Ancient Greek and Roman marble sculptures were once painted in bright colors, a practice called polychromy, Greek for 'many colors'.
Researchers use infrared and ultraviolet light to find traces of pigment on ancient statues.
Weathering, cleaning, air and sunlight erased most of ancient statues' original color.
The terra-cotta soldiers were once brightly painted; when first dug up, the lacquer under the paint could curl within 15 seconds and flake off in about four minutes.
Meketre's painted models are remarkably well preserved, with their original colors.

title: Byzantine gold mosaics
description: Byzantine mosaics like Justinian and Theodora at San Vitale set flat, stylized holy and imperial figures against gold glass, read as a spiritual realm rather than a real place.

facts.text: The church of San Vitale in Ravenna, Italy, was consecrated in 547; its apse mosaics of about that time show Emperor Justinian and Empress Theodora with their courts, facing each other.
In the San Vitale mosaic Justinian, haloed and in a purple robe, holds a golden paten, a dish for the Eucharist bread; opposite, Theodora holds a chalice for the wine.
The gold of Byzantine mosaics is glass: small cubes (tesserae) with a thin sheet of gold leaf sealed under a layer of clear glass.
Art historians read Byzantine gold backgrounds and flat, stylized figures as placing holy figures in a spiritual, otherworldly realm rather than a real setting.

title: Byzantine icons and Iconoclasm
description: An icon is an image of a holy figure, usually painted on a wooden panel; believers honored the person shown, and Byzantine emperors banned icon veneration from about 726 until 843.

facts.text: In art history, an icon usually means an image of a holy figure (Christ, Mary or a saint) painted on a wooden panel, in encaustic or egg tempera.

The icon of Christ at Saint Catherine's Monastery, Sinai, painted in the 6th century in encaustic (hot wax) on wood, is the oldest known panel icon of Christ; he blesses with one hand and holds a jeweled Gospel book.
Defenders of icons held that they did not worship the wood and paint: honor shown to an icon passed to the holy person it showed.
From about 726, Byzantine emperors condemned the veneration of icons as idolatry and countless images were destroyed; icons were restored for good in 843, still celebrated by the Orthodox Church.
The Sinai icon of Christ escaped the destruction of Iconoclasm because the monastery lay outside imperial control.

title: Figures and the mosque
description: Islamic religious spaces avoid images of people and animals, from the belief that creating living forms belongs to God; figures are common in secular Islamic art.

facts.text: Mosques and other Islamic religious buildings do not show people; Islamic religious art uses calligraphy, geometric pattern and arabesque (vegetal) designs instead.

Islamic resistance to images of living beings stems from the belief that creating living forms is unique to God; the Qur'an calls God musawwir, "maker of forms", and sayings attributed to the Prophet warn painters who try to "breathe life" into images.
Outside religious spaces, figures of people and animals are common in Islamic art, in palaces and in illustrated books.

title: Islamic calligraphy
description: Calligraphy is the most highly regarded Islamic art because Muslims believe the Qur'an, God's revelation, came in Arabic; the script decorates buildings and objects too.

facts.text: Calligraphy is the most highly regarded element of Islamic art, because the Qur'an, which Muslims believe is God's revelation to the Prophet Muhammad, was revealed in Arabic.
Islamic calligraphy decorates not only books but buildings and objects: mosque walls, ceramics, metalwork and textiles.

title: Islamic geometric pattern
description: Islamic geometric patterns are built from circles and straight lines with compass and ruler; repeated units can extend without end, which many read as suggesting infinity.

facts.text: Islamic geometric patterns are built from simple forms like the circle and square, drawn with just a compass and a ruler, and repeated from a single unit.
Because a repeated geometric unit can extend indefinitely, many scholars read Islamic patterns as suggesting infinity and, for some, the unity of God.

title: The Great Mosque of Córdoba
description: Begun about 785, its prayer hall is a forest of reused Roman columns carrying two tiers of arches striped in red brick and white stone.

facts.text: The Great Mosque of Córdoba, in Spain, was begun about 785 under the ruler Abd al-Rahman I.
The Great Mosque's prayer hall is a forest of columns, many reused from ancient Roman buildings, carrying two tiers of arches with alternating red brick and white stone.
At Córdoba, a second tier of arches stacked above the lower horseshoe arches gave the prayer hall greater height.

title: The Alhambra
description: The Nasrid palace-fortress in Granada, named "the red one", with the Court of the Lions, muqarnas ceilings and the motto "There is no victor but God" repeated on its walls.

facts.text: The name Alhambra comes from Arabic al-Hamra, "the red one", after the reddish color of its walls.
The Alhambra's famous palaces were built in the 14th century by the Nasrid sultans, the last Muslim dynasty to rule in Spain.
The Court of the Lions, built for the Nasrid sultan Muhammad V from 1362, centers on a fountain whose basin rests on 12 carved marble lions.
The Nasrid motto "There is no victor but God" is inscribed over and over across the Alhambra's walls.
The halls around the Court of the Lions have some of the most elaborate muqarnas vaults in the Islamic world: ceilings of many small niche-like cells, often compared to honeycomb.

title: How manuscripts were illuminated
description: Medieval books were handwritten on vellum, mostly in monasteries; strictly, illuminated means decorated with gold or silver leaf that was glued down and polished to shine.

facts.text: Strictly, an illuminated manuscript is a handwritten book decorated with gold or silver; the word comes from Latin illuminare, and today it covers any decorated manuscript.
The finest medieval manuscripts were written on vellum, a parchment made from calfskin.
Medieval manuscripts were mostly made in monasteries: a scribe ruled faint lines on the page, then wrote with a sharpened quill or reed pen.
Illuminators laid thin gold or silver leaf onto a sticky ground and polished it to a shine with a smooth stone or even a dog's tooth.

title: The Book of Kells
description: An illuminated Gospel book of about 800 made by Columban monks at Iona and Kells, famous for its Chi-Rho page, now at Trinity College Dublin.

facts.text: The Book of Kells, made about 800 by Columban monks, holds the four Gospels in Latin on 340 vellum leaves; it is kept at Trinity College Dublin.
Work on the Book of Kells probably began at the monastery on Iona, off Scotland; after a Viking raid in 806 the monks moved to Kells in Ireland.
The Book of Kells' Chi-Rho page is filled by the Greek letters Chi and Rho, the start of "Christ", with small cats and mice among the decoration.

title: Romanesque churches
description: Romanesque ("Roman-like") churches of about 1000 to 1150 used round arches and stone barrel vaults, whose outward push demanded thick walls and small windows.

facts.text: Romanesque, meaning "Roman-like", is a name coined by 19th-century scholars for European art and architecture of about 1000 to 1150, which borrowed the round arch from ancient Rome.
Romanesque churches used heavy stone barrel vaults, which push outward, so they needed massive walls with few, small windows, and their interiors were often dark.

title: Pilgrimage and the Conques tympanum
description: Pilgrimage churches like Sainte-Foy at Conques drew crowds to relics; its early-12th-century tympanum carves the Last Judgment over the door.

facts.text: Sainte-Foy at Conques, in France, was a stop for pilgrims on the way to Santiago de Compostela in Spain, drawn by the relics of Saint Foy.

The tympanum over Conques' west door, carved in the early 1100s, shows the Last Judgment with at least 124 figures: Christ sits in judgment, and below him the archangel Michael weighs souls while a devil presses on the scale.

title: How Gothic churches soar
description: Pointed arches, ribbed vaults and flying buttresses carried the roof's weight to piers and outside supports, so Gothic walls could be thin and full of windows.

facts.text: A pointed arch directs more of its load downward, and less outward, than a round arch, so it can rise higher.
A ribbed vault is a ceiling of stone ribs filled with thin stone panels; it is lighter than a solid vault and carries its weight down at a few points rather than along whole walls.
A flying buttress is a half arch outside the building that carries the outward push of the vault to an outer pier, letting walls become thinner and open into large windows.
Beauvais Cathedral's choir vault, about 48 meters high, is the tallest Gothic vault; part of it collapsed in 1284 and was rebuilt at the same height with extra supports.

title: Saint-Denis and the Gothic name
description: Gothic began with Abbot Suger's choir at Saint-Denis, dedicated in 1144 and meant to fill with light; Renaissance writers later used "Gothic" as an insult.

facts.text: The abbey church of Saint-Denis, near Paris, is traditionally called the first Gothic building; its new choir was dedicated in 1144.
Abbot Suger of Saint-Denis saw light as a reflection of the infinite light of God and wanted his new choir filled with it; his masons combined the pointed arch, ribbed vault and large windows.
Italian Renaissance writers such as Giorgio Vasari used the word Gothic as an insult, linking the style to the Goths, whom they saw as barbarians who helped destroy Rome.

title: How stained glass was made
description: Glass was colored with metal oxides while molten, cut into pieces, painted with dark paint fired onto the glass, and held together with strips of lead called cames.

facts.text: Medieval glassmakers colored glass by adding metal oxides to it while it was molten; cobalt, for example, gives deep blue.

Glaziers cut colored glass into pieces, painted details such as faces with a dark paint made partly of ground glass, fired it in a kiln to fuse it on, and joined the pieces with lead strips called cames.
The Sainte-Chapelle in Paris, a royal chapel consecrated in 1248 under King Louis IX, has 1,113 stained-glass scenes, mostly from the Bible, so many that its walls seem made of glass.

title: Windows that teach
description: Chartres' Belle Verrière survived the fire of 1194; Pope Gregory the Great's defense of pictures as books for those who cannot read became the standard Western defense of religious images.

facts.text: Fire destroyed most of Chartres Cathedral in 1194; the central panels of the Virgin and Child in the window called Notre-Dame de la Belle Verrière, from about 1180, survived and were set into the new building.
For centuries, the Belle Verrière's image of Mary has been an object of special veneration.
In a letter of 600, Pope Gregory the Great defended religious pictures: what writing gives those who read, a picture gives to those who cannot read.
Gregory's argument remained the standard defense of religious images in the Western church through the Middle Ages.

title: Giotto's Arena Chapel
description: About 1305 Giotto painted the Arena (Scrovegni) Chapel in Padua in fresco, with blue skies instead of gold; Dante noted his fame.

facts.text: About 1305 Giotto covered the walls of the Arena (Scrovegni) Chapel in Padua, paid for by the Scrovegni family, with scenes from the lives of the Virgin Mary and Christ.
Giotto painted in fresco: pigment brushed onto wet plaster, so the color dries into the wall.
In the Arena Chapel, Giotto painted blue skies rather than the traditional gold backgrounds.
In the Divine Comedy (Purgatorio, Canto 11), Dante wrote that Cimabue thought he held the field in painting, but now the cry is for Giotto, a lesson on how fast fame fades.

title: Giotto's solid, feeling figures
description: Giotto replaced flat Byzantine saints with rounded, weighty bodies that show emotion, as in the Lamentation.

facts.text: Giotto broke with the flat, stylized saints of Byzantine painting: his figures have rounded, sculptural bodies with a clear sense of weight, and they show real feeling.

In Giotto's Lamentation (about 1305), mourners surround the dead Christ, two figures in front sit with their backs to the viewer, a rocky ridge slopes down toward Christ's head, and angels grieve in the sky.

title: Chinese landscape painting
description: Shan shui ("mountain-water") painting flowered in the Northern Song; painters combined several viewpoints and used unpainted silk for mist.

facts.text: The Chinese term for landscape painting, shan shui, means "mountain-water".
Monumental landscape painting flowered in China's Northern Song dynasty (960–1127), in ink on silk or paper.
The court painter Guo Xi, of the 11th century, wrote of three distances in landscape: high (looking up at a peak), deep (peering into the valleys behind) and level (gazing across to far hills).
Guo Xi's Early Spring, dated 1072, combines the three distances in one picture instead of using a single fixed viewpoint.
Chinese landscape painters paid as much attention to unpainted areas as to painted ones; mist and cloud are often simply bare silk or paper.

title: Fan Kuan's Travelers among Mountains and Streams
description: A hanging scroll of about 1000, over 2 meters tall, where a huge mountain dwarfs a tiny mule train; Fan Kuan's signature was found hidden in the leaves in 1958.

facts.text: Fan Kuan's Travelers among Mountains and Streams, painted about 1000, is an ink hanging scroll on silk about 206 centimeters (over 2 meters) tall, in the National Palace Museum, Taipei.
In Fan Kuan's scroll a huge mountain fills most of the picture, and the travelers are a tiny mule train near the bottom.
In 1958 a scholar at the National Palace Museum spotted Fan Kuan's signature hidden among the leaves beside the mule train, settling doubts about who painted it.

title: Hagia Sophia: one building, two faiths
description: Built as Justinian's church in 532–537, Hagia Sophia became a mosque in 1453, a museum from 1934 and a mosque again in 2020; its mosaics and calligraphy share the space.

facts.text: Hagia Sophia in Constantinople (now Istanbul) was built as a church for Emperor Justinian from 532 to 537.
After the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II conquered Constantinople in 1453, Hagia Sophia became a mosque; minarets were added and many figural mosaics were plastered over.
Hagia Sophia was made a museum by a decree of 1934 and redesignated a mosque in 2020.
Huge round panels of Arabic calligraphy, naming God, Muhammad and the early caliphs, were hung in Hagia Sophia in the 19th century; many mosaics were uncovered again in the 1930s.

title: Why the Renaissance began in Florence
description: Florence, rich from cloth and banking, launched the Renaissance; its 1401 contest for Baptistery doors, won by Ghiberti over Brunelleschi, is often seen as a starting point.

facts.text: In 1401 Florence held a competition for bronze doors for its Baptistery; seven artists, including Ghiberti and Brunelleschi, each made a quatrefoil bronze relief of Abraham's sacrifice of Isaac.
Florence's 1401 Baptistery doors competition is often seen as a starting point of the Renaissance.
Florence grew rich from its cloth industry and banking, and its gold coin, the florin, became a monetary standard far beyond the city.
In Renaissance Florence, wealthy merchant families, chief among them the Medici, paid for building and decorating palaces, churches and monasteries.
Lorenzo Ghiberti won the Baptistery doors commission; work on his first doors ran from the 1403 contract until 1424.
Ghiberti's Baptistery doors were commissioned by the Calimala, a powerful Florentine merchants' guild.
After losing the 1401 doors competition to Ghiberti, Brunelleschi shifted his career toward architecture.

title: Renaissance humanism
description: Humanists studied classical Greek and Latin texts and made human nature and dignity their subject, part of the Renaissance's rebirth of antiquity.

facts.text: Renaissance humanism began in northern Italy in the 13th and 14th centuries; humanists studied classical Greek and Latin texts and took human nature and human dignity as their subject.

title: Linear perspective
description: Parallel lines receding into a picture converge at one vanishing point on the horizon line; Brunelleschi demonstrated it about 1415 and Alberti wrote it down in 1435.

facts.text: About 1415, Brunelleschi painted Florence's Baptistery, as seen from just inside the cathedral doorway, on a panel with a lentil-sized peephole; viewers looked through the back at a mirror held in front.
In Brunelleschi's test the painting, reflected in the mirror, could be compared directly with the real Baptistery and matched it; the panel itself is now lost.
In linear perspective, parallel lines receding into the picture converge at a single vanishing point on the horizon line, and objects get smaller as they approach it.
Leon Battista Alberti set out linear perspective in writing in his treatise On Painting (Della pittura) of 1435.

title: Masaccio's Holy Trinity
description: Masaccio's Holy Trinity (1425-27) used linear perspective so a painted vault seems to open a chapel into a flat wall.

facts.text: Masaccio's Holy Trinity fresco (1425-27) in Santa Maria Novella, Florence, shows Christ on the cross beneath a coffered barrel vault drawn in linear perspective, so the wall seems to open into a chapel.

title: The dome nobody could build
description: Florence Cathedral, begun in 1296, needed an eight-sided dome about 45 metres wide by 1418; Brunelleschi, a goldsmith, won the job in 1420.

facts.text: Construction of Florence Cathedral began in 1296.

By 1418 Florence Cathedral needed a vault over its eight-sided crossing, a problem that had challenged architects for decades; a competition was held that year and Brunelleschi's model was chosen in 1420.
Florence Cathedral's dome is about 45 metres wide.
Brunelleschi was a goldsmith with no serious architectural training.

title: How Brunelleschi built the dome
description: Brunelleschi built the dome (1420-36) without centering, using a double shell and self-supporting herringbone brickwork; it is still the largest masonry dome.

facts.text: Centering is a temporary wooden framework that supports an arch, vault or dome while it is built and is removed once the mortar has set.
Brunelleschi's dome was built from 1420 to 1436 without centering or formwork; a system of measuring wires kept its curves true.
Brunelleschi's dome has two layers: an inner shell spanning the space and an outer shell protecting it from the weather.
Brunelleschi set some bricks at angles to the others in a herringbone pattern that locked each new course to the ones below, so the dome supported itself as it rose.
Florence Cathedral's dome is still the largest masonry dome in the world.
Brunelleschi's design for the lantern on top of the dome was approved in 1436, but it was completed after his death in 1446.

title: Patrons and contracts
description: Renaissance art was usually paid for by patrons who set pay, materials, deadline and subject by contract, down to the price of ultramarine blue.

facts.text: A patron is the person paying for a work of art; Renaissance patrons often set the pay, materials, deadline and subject in a contract with the artist.
In October 1485 the prior of Florence's foundling hospital contracted Domenico Ghirlandaio to paint an Adoration of the Magi himself, following an approved drawing, within 30 months, for 115 florins.
Ghirlandaio's 1485 contract required him to use ultramarine costing 4 florins an ounce.
Ultramarine was made from lapis lazuli, a stone mined in north-eastern Afghanistan, and was the most expensive blue pigment.

title: The Medici as patrons
description: The Medici, rich from banking and cloth, paid for art that sometimes pictured them, and Lorenzo took the young Michelangelo into his household.

facts.text: The Medici family's fortune came from cloth manufacturing and banking.

Benozzo Gozzoli's Procession of the Magi (1459-60), chosen by Cosimo de' Medici, spreads the Magi's procession of riders through a landscape of trees and flowering meadows across three walls of the Medici palace chapel, with Medici family portraits among them.
Lorenzo de' Medici, the Magnificent, a poet and patron, took the young Michelangelo into his household, where he could study the Medici collection of ancient Roman sculpture fragments.
At 13, Michelangelo was apprenticed to the painter Domenico Ghirlandaio.

title: Leonardo's notebooks
description: Thousands of pages of Leonardo's notes survive, in left-handed mirror writing, on anatomy, machines and flight, with drawings leading the words.

facts.text: Thousands of pages of Leonardo's notebooks survive, written in mirror writing that runs from right to left; he was left-handed, which made mirror writing easier.
Leonardo's notebooks cover subjects including anatomy, mechanics and flight, and in them the drawings take precedence, with the words explaining them.
Leonardo divided his energy between art and science and finished surprisingly few paintings.

title: Leonardo's painting
description: Leonardo's Mona Lisa uses sfumato, soft shading with no outlines; his experimental Last Supper began deteriorating in his lifetime.

facts.text: The Mona Lisa is a half-length portrait of a woman in a three-quarter pose with folded hands, set against a distant landscape of valleys and rivers.
Sfumato, from the Italian for 'to evaporate like smoke', is fine shading that makes soft transitions between tones without lines or borders; Leonardo is its most famous user.
Leonardo's Last Supper (1495-98), on the refectory wall of Santa Maria delle Grazie in Milan, shows Christ announcing that one of the apostles will betray him, and their reactions.
For the Last Supper Leonardo abandoned true fresco on wet plaster and painted in tempera on a dry wall; the painting was already deteriorating in his lifetime.

title: Michelangelo's David
description: Michelangelo carved the David (1501-04) from an abandoned block; it shows David before the battle and became a symbol of Florence's republic.

facts.text: The marble block for the David had been started and rejected by earlier sculptors, Agostino di Duccio in 1464 and Antonio Rossellino in 1475, and lay abandoned for about 25 years.
Michelangelo carved the David from 1501 to 1504, starting at age 26.
Michelangelo's David is a marble nude 5.17 metres tall, standing with his weight on one leg (contrapposto), with a nearly invisible sling and watchful eyes.
Earlier Florentine artists showed David triumphant over Goliath; Michelangelo's David is usually read as David before the battle, concentrating.
A committee including Leonardo da Vinci placed the David in Florence's Piazza della Signoria as a symbol of republican liberty; it moved to the Accademia in 1873.

title: The Sistine Chapel ceiling
description: Michelangelo, a sculptor at heart, painted the Sistine ceiling (1508-12) standing on scaffolding; it includes the Creation of Adam's nearly touching fingers.

facts.text: Pope Julius II commissioned the Sistine Chapel ceiling, which Michelangelo painted from 1508 to 1512.
Michelangelo thought of himself primarily as a sculptor and had no fresco experience when he was given the Sistine ceiling.
Michelangelo painted the Sistine ceiling standing on scaffolding he designed, not lying on his back; the myth probably comes from the 1965 film The Agony and the Ecstasy.
Nine scenes from the Book of Genesis run down the center of the Sistine Chapel ceiling.
In Michelangelo's Creation of Adam, Adam lounges on the ground and lifts a limp hand while God, borne by angels in swirling drapery, reaches toward him; their fingers almost touch.

title: Raphael's School of Athens
description: Raphael's School of Athens gathers Greek philosophers in a classical hall, with Plato and Aristotle at the central vanishing point.

facts.text: Raphael painted The School of Athens, a fresco of ancient Greek philosophers, in the Vatican's Stanza della Segnatura about 1509-11, while Michelangelo was painting the nearby Sistine ceiling.
The School of Athens sets its philosophers in a vast hall of arches and barrel vaults said to be based on Bramante's design for the new St. Peter's.
At the center of The School of Athens, Plato points up to the sky and Aristotle gestures down toward the earth.
In The School of Athens, Heraclitus, leaning on a block of marble, is a portrait of Michelangelo, and the figure at far right in a black beret is Raphael himself.
In The School of Athens, Plato and Aristotle stand at the architecture's central vanishing point.

title: High Renaissance balance
description: The High Renaissance (1490s-1520s) aimed at balance and harmony, as in Raphael's triangle-based Madonna in the Meadow.

facts.text: The Renaissance reached its height between the 1490s and the 1520s, a period called the High Renaissance, whose ideal was perfect balance and harmony.
In Raphael's Madonna in the Meadow (1505/06), Mary sits on the ground with the infant Jesus and the young John the Baptist, and the group fits inside an equilateral triangle.
Raphael died at 37, in 1520, yet for centuries he was recognised as the supreme High Renaissance painter.

title: Oil paint versus tempera
description: Egg tempera dries fast and is shaded by crosshatching; slow-drying oil lets tones blend in thin glazes, a technique van Eyck perfected.

facts.text: True tempera binds pigment with egg yolk; it dries quickly, so painters shaded with fine crosshatched strokes instead of blending.
Oil paint is pigment mixed with a drying oil such as linseed; it dries slowly, so tones can be blended and laid in thin, see-through glazes.
Jan van Eyck did not invent oil painting but perfected the newly developed technique, using thin transparent glazes.
By the 16th century, in Venice, oil paint had become painters' basic material.
Leonardo's sfumato in the Mona Lisa, built from thin translucent layers, was made possible by oil paint, then relatively new in Italy.

title: Van Eyck's Arnolfini Portrait
description: Van Eyck's Arnolfini Portrait (1434) shows a couple in Bruges, a convex mirror reflecting the room, and the signature 'Jan van Eyck was here'.

facts.text: Jan van Eyck's Arnolfini Portrait is signed above its mirror 'Johannes de Eyck fuit hic. 1434', Latin for 'Jan van Eyck was here. 1434'.
The Arnolfini Portrait shows a richly dressed man and woman, probably the Italian merchant Giovanni di Nicolao Arnolfini and his wife, in a room in Bruges with a red bed and a brass chandelier.
The convex mirror in the Arnolfini Portrait reflects the room, the couple from behind and two men coming in at the door; who the men are, and whether one is the artist, is debated.
In 1449 an Italian humanist wrote that van Eyck's works seemed made not by human hands but by nature herself.

title: Woodcut and engraving
description: A woodcut prints from a raised design left after cutting away wood; an engraving prints from ink held in lines cut into a metal plate.

facts.text: A woodcut is a relief print: the parts of the wood block that should not print are cut away, leaving the design raised to take the ink.
Engraving is an intaglio process: lines are cut into a metal plate with a sharp tool called a burin, and after inking the surface is wiped clean so only the ink in the grooves prints.

title: Prints spread images
description: A block or plate prints the same picture again and again; after Gutenberg's press, prints like Dürer's carried images across Europe.

facts.text: Once a block or plate is prepared, a printed picture can be repeated over and over with little loss of detail.
Johannes Gutenberg built Europe's first known mechanized printing press and printed the Gutenberg Bible around 1455, making large numbers of books cheap to produce.
On his first trip to Italy, in 1494-95, Dürer studied engravings by Italian masters.
Dürer's Apocalypse woodcuts, published in 1498, made him famous, including across the Alps in Italy.

title: Dürer's Rhinoceros
description: Dürer's 1515 Rhinoceros, made without seeing the animal, gave it armor plates and stayed Europe's standard rhino image into the 1700s.

facts.text: In 1515 the German artist Albrecht Dürer made his Rhinoceros woodcut without ever seeing the animal, working from a letter's description and a sketch of an Indian rhinoceros that had arrived in Lisbon.

Dürer's Rhinoceros shows armor-like plates and an extra horn on its back; copied into natural history books, it stayed Europe's standard rhino image until a touring rhino named Clara became a sensation in the 1700s.

title: Naming the Renaissance
description: Vasari's Lives (1550) described a rinascita of art; 'Renaissance' as the name of an era came from Michelet in 1855.

facts.text: Giorgio Vasari, a painter and architect who designed the Uffizi, published his Lives of the painters, sculptors and architects in 1550, revised in 1568; it is seen as the first modern art history.
Vasari told art's story in three periods (classical excellence, medieval decline and a rebirth, or rinascita, beginning in 14th-century Tuscany), with Michelangelo as the peak.
Vasari's Lives favored Italian, especially Tuscan, artists and sometimes included unverified anecdotes.
'Renaissance' as the name of a historical period came in the 19th century: Jules Michelet used it in 1855, and Jacob Burckhardt's influential 1860 book spread it.

title: Baroque drama
description: Baroque art, from Italy about 1600, used movement, diagonals and emotion to grab the viewer; the name began as an insult meaning a misshapen pearl.

facts.text: The word Baroque probably comes from the Portuguese barroco, an irregularly shaped pearl; for centuries critics used it to mean odd or overdone.
The Baroque began in Italy in the late 1500s and roughly coincides with the 17th century.
Rubens's Elevation of the Cross (about 1610), for Antwerp's cathedral, shows muscular men straining to raise the cross, which cuts across the picture on a diagonal.
Rubens's stormy diagonal compositions and full-blooded figures are seen as the essence of Baroque painting.

title: Art to stir faith
description: After the Council of Trent (1545-63), the Catholic Church wanted clear, dramatic art to strengthen ordinary people's faith, which drove the Baroque.

facts.text: After the Council of Trent (1545 to 1563), the Catholic Church wanted art to strengthen the public's faith: clear, lifelike images with dramatic effects to stir devotion.

title: Pozzo's painted dome
description: In 1685 Andrea Pozzo painted a fake dome on a flat surface in Sant'Ignazio, Rome; a disc in the floor marks where the illusion works.

facts.text: In 1685 Andrea Pozzo painted a fake dome on a flat surface in Rome's church of Sant'Ignazio; the Jesuits had apparently run out of money for a real one.
A disc set in Sant'Ignazio's floor marks the spot where the painted dome looks real; from elsewhere the illusion breaks.

title: Chiaroscuro and tenebrism
description: Chiaroscuro (light-dark) uses light and shadow to make things look solid; tenebrism, its harshest form, was pioneered by Caravaggio.

facts.text: Chiaroscuro, from the Italian chiaro (light) and scuro (dark), uses light and shadow to make objects look three-dimensional.
Tenebrism is chiaroscuro at its most intense, with harsh light picking figures out of darkness; Caravaggio and his followers pioneered it.

title: Caravaggio's light and real people
description: Caravaggio's Calling of Saint Matthew uses a beam of light to tell the story, and his saints were modeled on ordinary people, dirty feet and all.

facts.text: In Caravaggio's Calling of Saint Matthew (about 1600), in a chapel in Rome, men sit counting coins at a table as Christ, at the right, points at Matthew.
In The Calling of Saint Matthew, a beam of light crosses the dark room to the faces at the table, pointing at Matthew as Christ's hand does.
In the painting, a man at the table points to himself, as if to ask whether Christ means him.
Caravaggio painted holy figures from ordinary people in the clothes of his day, with ragged clothing and dirty feet; some viewers resisted it.
Caravaggio's style influenced later painters, including Rembrandt and Velázquez.

title: Bernini's marble in motion
description: Bernini froze stories mid-action in marble: David about to throw, with the viewer in Goliath's place, and Daphne turning into a tree.

facts.text: Bernini's marble David (1623 to 1624) twists in the instant before he hurls the stone at Goliath.
Bernini's David was meant to put the viewer where Goliath would stand, drawn into the action.
According to early sources, David's face is Bernini's own.
Bernini's Apollo and Daphne (1622 to 1625) shows Daphne turning into a laurel tree: roots at her feet, leaves at her fingers, bark under Apollo's hand.

title: Bernini's St. Peter's Square
description: Bernini's curving colonnades (1656-67) wrap St. Peter's Square like embracing arms; from two discs, four rows of columns line up as one.

facts.text: Bernini designed the colonnades of St. Peter's Square (1656 to 1667): 284 columns in four rows, curving around the square.
The curving colonnades symbolize the Church's arms embracing the faithful.
From either of two marble discs in the square's pavement, the four rows of columns line up and look like a single row.

title: The Night Watch
description: Rembrandt's 1642 militia company portrait, named for darkened varnish, turned a stiff group portrait into a scene of light and action.

facts.text: Rembrandt's The Night Watch (1642) is a daytime scene; the name, first recorded in 1797, came from thick, darkened varnish.
The Night Watch is a portrait of an Amsterdam militia company under Captain Frans Banninck Cocq.
In The Night Watch, the captain in black with a red sash strides beside his lieutenant in pale cream, and a glowing girl in yellow, the company's mascot, stands behind.
Rembrandt used strong chiaroscuro and a lively, theatrical arrangement instead of the usual static rows of a group portrait.

title: Rembrandt's self-portraits
description: About 80 Rembrandt self-portraits survive from 40 years; suggested reasons include practicing expressions, testing light and selling to collectors.

facts.text: About 80 self-portraits by Rembrandt survive (paintings, etchings and drawings) from a 40-year career, far more than any other painter of his time.
In a self-portrait of about 1628, painted at about 22, Rembrandt let light glance along one cheek while the rest of his face sits in shadow.
In his Self Portrait at the Age of 63 (1669), from the year he died, thick paint builds the sagging, blotchy skin of his old face.
Suggested reasons for Rembrandt's self-portraits include practicing expressions, experimenting with light and selling to collectors.

title: No pictures in Dutch churches
description: Calvinist teaching banned images in Dutch churches, so painters lost the church commissions that fed art elsewhere.

facts.text: In the Dutch Republic, Calvinist teaching banned images in churches, though not in homes or civic buildings.

Elsewhere in Europe, artists could hope for big commissions from the church or state; the Dutch Republic instead had a growing independent market, where painters made pictures to sell rather than to order.

title: Painting for the open market
description: Dutch painters sold ready-made pictures to ordinary households and specialized in subjects like still life to find a niche.

facts.text: In 1640 English traveller Peter Mundy wrote that in Amsterdam even blacksmiths and cobblers kept a picture by their forge or in their stall.
Some Dutch oil paintings cost less than household linen or a piece of furniture, within reach of ordinary citizens.
An estimated 1.3 to 1.4 million paintings were made in the Netherlands in the 20 years from 1640 to 1659, for a population of about 2 million.
Dutch painters often specialized in one subject, such as landscape or still life, to build a reputation and a profitable niche.
Willem Claesz. Heda, a Haarlem still-life specialist, painted oysters, a lemon, a tall glass and a silver bowl in 1634, full of gleaming reflections.

title: Vermeer and The Milkmaid
description: Only about 36 Vermeers survive; The Milkmaid shows a still kitchen lit from a window, with light built from hundreds of colored dots.

facts.text: Only about 36 paintings by Vermeer, who worked in Delft, survive.
Vermeer was little known outside his region until the 1800s, when the critic Théophile Thoré brought him international fame.
In Vermeer's The Milkmaid (about 1660), a maid pours milk into a bowl beside bread on a table, lit by a window on the left; except for the milk, everything is still.
Vermeer showed light playing over the objects in The Milkmaid with hundreds of small colored dots of paint.

title: Did Vermeer use a camera obscura?
description: Vermeer's blurred light spots match what a camera obscura shows, but no document proves he used one, so it stays a debated idea.

facts.text: Vermeer's small blurred light spots, like those on the bread in The Milkmaid, match effects seen in a camera obscura, a device that projects an image.
No document from Vermeer's time shows he owned or used a camera obscura, so the idea is debated.

title: Las Meninas
description: Velázquez's 1656 painting of the young infanta, her maids of honor and the painter himself at a huge canvas, by the king's own painter.

facts.text: From 1623 Velázquez worked for King Philip IV of Spain as the only painter allowed to paint the king.

Las Meninas (1656) shows the five-year-old Infanta Margarita Teresa, daughter of Philip IV, at the center with her maids of honor (meninas), two people with dwarfism and a large dog lying on the floor.
In Las Meninas, Velázquez painted himself at the left, brush in hand, before a large canvas whose front we cannot see.

title: The mirror in Las Meninas
description: A mirror reflects the king and queen, leaving open what Velázquez is painting and where the viewer stands: a painting about painting.

facts.text: A mirror on the back wall of Las Meninas reflects King Philip IV and Queen Mariana.
Las Meninas leaves open what Velázquez is painting and where the viewer stands; one reading puts the king and queen where you stand, and it is often called a painting about painting.

title: Rococo
description: Rococo began in early-1700s Paris as a lighter reaction to Louis XIV's Baroque: shell-like curves, pastels and playful love scenes, later attacked as frivolous.

facts.text: Rococo began in early-1700s Paris as a reaction against the heavy Baroque of Louis XIV's reign, and flourished about 1700 to 1770.
The name Rococo comes from the French rocaille, the shell-covered rockwork used to decorate artificial grottoes.
Rococo favored curving C and S shapes, light pastels, ivory white and gold, and lighthearted scenes of myth and courtship.
By the 1750s and 1760s critics attacked Rococo as frivolous, and the stricter Neoclassical style gradually replaced it in France.

title: Fragonard's The Swing
description: In The Swing (about 1767-68) a woman in pink flies up between an older man and a hidden lover, her slipper in the air: Rococo at its most playful.

facts.text: In Fragonard's The Swing (about 1767 to 1768), a young woman in pink silk flies up between an older man pushing the swing and a young lover in the bushes; one slipper flies off.
According to a 1767 account, a gentleman of the court asked the painter Doyen for his mistress on a swing pushed by a bishop; Doyen refused and passed the job to Fragonard.

title: Why Neoclassicism looked back
description: Digs at Herculaneum and Pompeii and Winckelmann's praise of Greek art turned artists from Rococo toward calm, clear ancient models.

facts.text: Neoclassicism flourished about 1760 to 1860, peaking in the 1780s and 1790s, as a reaction against Rococo.
Excavations at Herculaneum (from 1738) and Pompeii (from 1748) fed the new interest in ancient art.
Mount Vesuvius buried the Roman city of Pompeii under ash and pumice in 79 CE; digging in the 1700s revealed a city frozen in time.
The scholar Johann Joachim Winckelmann praised Greek art's 'noble simplicity and quiet grandeur' and urged artists to imitate it.
Neoclassical painting preferred line over color and straight lines over curves.

title: The Oath of the Horatii
description: David's 1784 painting of three Roman brothers swearing to fight for Rome became a manifesto for stern, clear Neoclassical art.

facts.text: In Jacques-Louis David's Oath of the Horatii (1784), three Roman brothers stretch out their arms and swear before their father, who holds up their swords, to fight for Rome, while the women of the family grieve.
David painted the Oath with firm outlines, bare space, sober color, a frieze-like row of figures and clear light.
Shown in Paris in 1785, the Oath caused a sensation as a manifesto for reviving art; later it was read as a call for stern, patriotic republican morals.

title: Who paid for art, 1600 to 1800
description: In this chapter three kinds of buyer shaped what got made: the Catholic Church, the Dutch open market, and kings and courtiers.

facts.text: From about 1600 to 1800, Western art was paid for by the Catholic Church, by buyers on the Dutch open market, and by kings and courtiers.

title: Baroque to Neoclassicism on the art clock
description: On Level 1's one-day clock of art history, everything from Caravaggio to David happens in the last ten minutes before midnight.

facts.text: On a 24-hour clock of the 67,800 years since the oldest known cave art, a work of about 1600 lands about 9 minutes before midnight and one of 1784 about 5 minutes before.

title: Romanticism
description: From the late 1700s to the mid-1800s, Romantic artists put emotion, imagination and the individual first, reacting against Enlightenment reason and Neoclassical order.

facts.text: Caspar David Friedrich's Wanderer above the Sea of Fog, completed about 1817, shows a man with his back to the viewer on a rocky peak above a sea of mist.
Because the wanderer is seen from behind (a Rückenfigur), viewers are invited to share his view of the landscape.
Romanticism, from the late 18th to the mid-19th century, put emotion over reason and valued imagination and the individual.
Romanticism was partly a reaction against the Enlightenment's trust in reason and order, and against Neoclassicism.
Friedrich believed a painter should paint not only what he has in front of him but also what he sees inside himself; the Wanderer combines sketches of several places.
In 1816 the French frigate Medusa ran aground off West Africa; about 150 people were set adrift on a raft, and after 13 days only 15 survived.
Géricault painted The Raft of the Medusa in 1818-19 on a canvas about 5 by 7 meters, after meeting survivors and using a scale model of the raft.
Instead of an ancient, noble subject, Géricault painted a recent, real disaster.
In The Raft of the Medusa, the bodies form a pyramid rising to a man waving a cloth at a tiny ship on the horizon.
At the 1819 Salon, The Raft of the Medusa divided critics: some were captivated, others repulsed.

title: The sublime
description: Edmund Burke (1757) described the sublime: awe mixed with terror at things vast, rugged and powerful. Romantic painters sought it in nature.

facts.text: In 1757 Edmund Burke linked the beautiful to smallness and smoothness, and the sublime to vastness, ruggedness and power, which stir awe mixed with terror.
Friedrich's Wanderer is often read as an image of the sublime power of nature.

title: Goya's dark turn
description: Goya rose to first court painter, went deaf after an 1792 illness, and turned to biting satire and, at the end, the Black Paintings on his own walls.

facts.text: Goya became painter to the king of Spain in 1786 and first court painter in 1799.
An illness in 1792 left Goya permanently deaf; afterward his work turned darker and more critical.
In 1799 Goya published Los Caprichos, 80 etchings attacking political, social and religious abuses; they were withdrawn from sale after a few days.
In The Sleep of Reason Produces Monsters, from Los Caprichos, the artist sleeps at his desk while owls and bats swarm around him.
Between about 1819 and 1823, Goya painted 14 dark murals, the Black Paintings, on the walls of his house outside Madrid, the Quinta del Sordo.
One Black Painting shows the wild-eyed god Saturn devouring one of his children.
After a new owner bought the house in 1873, the Black Paintings were transferred to canvas; they are now in the Prado.

title: The Third of May 1808
description: Goya's 1814 painting of French soldiers executing Madrid citizens: a lit man in a white shirt faces a faceless firing squad.

facts.text: Goya's The Third of May 1808, completed in 1814, shows French troops executing Spanish insurgents in Madrid during Napoleon's occupation.
In The Third of May 1808, a lantern lights a man in a white shirt with his arms raised in a Christlike pose, wounds like stigmata on his palms.
Goya shows the firing squad as a faceless, uniform row, unlike the individual victims.

title: Landscape's low rank
description: The academies ranked subjects: history painting at the top, landscape and still life at the bottom because they lacked human subject matter.

facts.text: The French Royal Academy ranked subjects: history painting first, then portrait, everyday scenes, landscape and still life.
History painting ranked highest because it showed noble events of history and religion; landscape and still life ranked lowest because they had no human subject.

title: Constable
description: John Constable painted his native Stour valley, studied skies outdoors, and won a Paris gold medal for The Hay Wain.

facts.text: Constable's The Hay Wain (1821) shows an empty hay wagon crossing the shallow millpond at Flatford on the River Stour.
The Hay Wain failed to sell when shown in London in 1821, but at the 1824 Paris Salon it won Constable a gold medal from King Charles X.
Constable, born in East Bergholt, Suffolk, painted the Stour valley countryside where he grew up.
Constable painted The Hay Wain in his London studio, working from outdoor sketches made over several years.
In 1821 and 1822 on Hampstead Heath, Constable painted dozens of cloud studies ("skying"), noting the date, time and wind on the back.

title: Turner
description: J.M.W. Turner painted storms, steam and speed so loosely that sea, sky and light merge.

facts.text: Turner's Snow Storm (about 1842) shows a steamboat tossed in a swirling vortex where water and light merge.
Turner claimed he had himself lashed to a ship's mast for four hours to watch the storm, but the story is doubted.
Some critics dismissed Snow Storm as "soapsuds and whitewash".
In Turner's Rain, Steam and Speed (1844), a steam train rushes toward the viewer across a bridge through the rain.

title: Courbet and Realism
description: Realism (about 1850-80) showed contemporary, ordinary life without prettying it; Courbet painted a village funeral at history-painting size.

facts.text: Courbet's A Burial at Ornans (1849-50), about 3 by 7 meters, shows more than 40 life-size people at a funeral in his small hometown.
A Burial at Ornans shows no angels and no heaven, just mourners around a hole in the ground, and its size and ordinary subject perplexed visitors to the Salon of 1850-51.
Realism, a movement in France from about 1850 to 1880, aimed to show contemporary life accurately, without embellishment, especially ordinary and humble people.
Realists rejected both the classical and the Romantic styles taught by the academies.
Courbet was the first artist to proclaim Realism openly as a program.
Canvases as huge as A Burial at Ornans were traditionally reserved for history and religious painting.
Courbet's The Stone Breakers (1849) showed a young man and an old man breaking stones by a road, and its frank plainness shocked public and critics.
The Stone Breakers was destroyed in the bombing of Dresden in February 1945 and is known today only from photographs and copies.
In 1855, after the Paris world's fair rejected his huge painting The Studio, Courbet showed it in his own pavilion labeled "Realism".

title: Millet's Gleaners
description: Millet's The Gleaners (1857) shows three peasant women picking up leftover grain, painted with a grandeur that unsettled wealthy viewers.

facts.text: Millet's The Gleaners (1857) shows three peasant women bent over a field, gathering stray stalks of grain left after the harvest.
Gleaning, picking up the grain left after a harvest, was an old right of the rural poor.
Behind the gleaners, Millet painted huge grain stacks and a heavily loaded wagon.
Millet was one of the first artists to paint peasant laborers with a grandeur once reserved for important people.
Shown less than ten years after the revolution of 1848, The Gleaners was read by many middle- and upper-class viewers as a threat.

title: Photography arrives
description: Niépce made the oldest surviving photo in 1826 or 1827; Daguerre's faster daguerreotype was announced in 1839, and painting had to rethink its job.

facts.text: In Daguerre's view of the Boulevard du Temple (about 1838), the long exposure erased moving traffic; only a man having his boots shined stood still long enough to appear.
The oldest surviving camera photograph, made by Nicéphore Niépce in 1826 or 1827, needed an exposure of hours, perhaps days.
Daguerre, once Niépce's partner, developed a much faster process; the daguerreotype was announced at the Academy of Sciences in Paris on January 9, 1839.
Each daguerreotype was a one-of-a-kind image on a polished, silver-plated copper plate, with no negative to print copies from.
The painter Paul Delaroche is reported to have declared, on seeing the daguerreotype, "From today, painting is dead."

title: Muybridge's galloping horse
description: In 1878 Muybridge's row of cameras showed a galloping horse lifts all four hooves with legs tucked under, disproving painters' "flying gallop".

facts.text: Painters long showed galloping horses in a "flying gallop", legs stretched out front and back, as in Géricault's Epsom Derby of 1821.
Hired by the railroad magnate Leland Stanford, Eadweard Muybridge photographed a galloping horse in 1878 with a row of cameras.
Muybridge's photos showed a galloping horse does lift all four hooves off the ground, but with its legs tucked under its body, not stretched out.
Some people refused to believe Muybridge's photos, thinking a horse's legs could never take such positions.

title: The first Impressionist show
description: In 1874 painters shut out of the Salon held their own show; a critic mocking Monet's Impression, Sunrise gave them their name.

facts.text: In April 1874, painters rejected by the official Salon held their own exhibition in Paris, in the photographer Nadar's former studio.
Critic Louis Leroy, mocking Monet's Impression, Sunrise, called the group "impressionists" in a satirical review in April 1874, and the name stuck.
Monet's Impression, Sunrise (1872) shows the harbor at Le Havre in the early morning: cranes, masts and smokestacks, rowboats, and an orange sun reflected in the water.
Leroy wrote that wallpaper in its early stages was more finished than Impression, Sunrise.
By the 1870s the Impressionists were consistently rejected by the Salon; after 1874 they held seven more shows, up to 1886.

title: How Impressionists painted
description: Impressionists painted outdoors in front of the scene, in dabs of pure color, with complementary colors in the shadows, to catch light at a given moment.

facts.text: Instead of finishing landscapes in the studio from sketches, Impressionists such as Monet painted entirely outdoors, in front of the scene.
Impressionists tried to record colors and forms as they appeared in natural light at a given time.
In 1841 the American painter John Goffe Rand patented a squeezable tin paint tube; before, painters stored paint in pig bladders.
Paint tubes are often said to have made Impressionism possible, but painters had worked outdoors for decades, with portable easels and paint boxes.
Impressionists built pictures from flecks and dabs of pure color placed side by side.
Impressionists stopped using grays and blacks for shadows and used complementary colors instead.

title: Monet's series
description: Monet painted the same motif again and again, grainstacks and then Rouen Cathedral, to catch changing light.

facts.text: Between late summer 1890 and February 1891, Monet painted 25 pictures of the same grainstacks in a field near his home at Giverny.
Each grainstack canvas catches different light, weather and season, from end of summer to snow and sunset; Monet switched canvases as the light changed.
In May 1891 Monet showed 15 grainstacks at his dealer's gallery in Paris to acclaim; they were his first series, meant to be seen together.
In 1892 and 1893 Monet painted Rouen Cathedral's front about 30 times from rooms across the square, switching canvases as the light moved.

title: Monet's water lilies
