description: Monet's last subject was his own water-lily pond at Giverny: almost 300 paintings, the largest hung in oval rooms at the Orangerie.

facts.text: Monet moved to Giverny in 1883 and created a water-lily pond there that became the subject of his last series.
Monet's Water Lilies cycle numbers almost 300 paintings, more than 40 of them very large.
The day after the 1918 Armistice, Monet offered water-lily panels to France; they were hung in two oval rooms at the Orangerie in 1927, months after his death.
Monet wanted the rooms to give "the illusion of an endless whole, of a wave with no horizon and no shore."

title: Degas and modern life
description: Degas, who preferred to call himself a realist, painted dancers backstage and Paris cafés from unusual, off-center viewpoints.

facts.text: At least half of Degas's mature work shows dance: about 1,500 paintings, pastels, prints and drawings of dancers.
Few of Degas's dance pictures show a performance; most show classes, rehearsals and the wings of the Paris Opera.
Degas's dim rehearsal rooms and gaslit stages set him apart from Monet and Pissarro, who responded to sunlight rather than gaslight.
Degas helped organize the first Impressionist exhibition in 1874, but he disliked the name and preferred to call himself a realist.
Degas scorned painting landscapes outdoors and preferred working in the studio from drawings.
Degas used extreme viewpoints and radical perspective to show modern Paris.
In Degas's L'Absinthe (1875-76), a woman stares blankly at a glass of absinthe beside a man in a hat who looks away, in a Paris café.
In L'Absinthe, Degas pushed the couple off-center, leaving a large empty foreground of café tables.
Degas's models for L'Absinthe were the actress Ellen Andrée and the artist Marcellin Desboutin, and critics called the painting disgusting.

title: Little Dancer Aged Fourteen
description: Degas's wax Little Dancer (1881) wore a real tutu, ribbon and hair, and outraged viewers used to idealized marble.

facts.text: Degas's wax Little Dancer Aged Fourteen, shown in 1881, wore a real tulle tutu and silk hair ribbon, with a wig of real hair.
The model for the Little Dancer was Marie van Goethem, a student of the Paris Opera ballet.
Viewers used to sculptures of idealized women in marble were outraged by the Little Dancer.

title: Berthe Morisot
description: A founding Impressionist, Morisot painted private moments of women and children, like The Cradle, and once outsold Monet and Renoir.

facts.text: At an 1875 auction in Paris, Berthe Morisot's works sold for more than those of Monet, Renoir and Sisley.
Morisot was a founding Impressionist and showed in all but one of the eight Impressionist exhibitions, missing 1879 just after her daughter Julie was born.
Morisot's The Cradle (1872), shown at the first Impressionist exhibition in 1874, shows her sister Edma watching her sleeping baby through the cradle's thin curtain.
Morisot painted mainly women and children indoors, in gardens and in parks near her home, with quick brushstrokes.

title: Mary Cassatt
description: The American Cassatt joined the Impressionists at Degas's invitation and painted women and children with unsentimental directness.

facts.text: After the Salon rejected Mary Cassatt's entries in 1877, Degas visited her studio and invited her to exhibit with the Impressionists; she first did so in 1879.
Cassatt was the only American officially part of the Impressionist group.
In Cassatt's Little Girl in a Blue Armchair (1878) a child sprawls across a big armchair, and Degas worked on the background.
Cassatt's The Child's Bath (1893) looks down from above at a woman washing a child's feet in a basin, their heads touching.
Social rules of the time limited where women artists like Cassatt and Morisot could go and whom they could paint, so they turned to family, friends and private spaces.

title: The Paris Salon
description: The Salon was France's official, jury-selected art show; rejected artists answered with the Salon des Refusés and independent exhibitions.

facts.text: The Salon, the official art exhibition sponsored by the French government, began in 1667, became annual after 1737 and used a selection jury from 1748.
In 1863 Emperor Napoleon III ordered a Salon des Refusés for works the official jury had rejected; Manet's Le Déjeuner sur l'herbe caused a scandal there.
After 1881, as independent exhibitions of avant-garde art grew more important, the Salon gradually lost its influence and prestige.

title: Post-Impressionism: one name, many directions
description: Roger Fry named Post-Impressionism in 1910 for painters, including Cézanne, Gauguin, Seurat and Van Gogh, who each took Impressionism in a different direction.

facts.text: The critic Roger Fry first used the term Post-Impressionism in 1910, for his London exhibition Manet and the Post-Impressionists.
Fry's label grouped very different painters, including Cézanne, Gauguin, Seurat and Van Gogh, each responding to Impressionism in their own way.
Georges Seurat tried to put Impressionist painting of light and color on a scientific basis, placing tiny dots of color side by side.

title: Cézanne's structure
description: Cézanne turned from Impressionism's effects of light to the underlying structure of natural forms, advising painters to treat nature by the cylinder, the sphere and the cone.

facts.text: Cézanne moved away from Impressionism's effects of light to focus on the underlying structure of natural forms.
In a letter of 15 April 1904 to the painter Émile Bernard, Cézanne advised treating nature by the cylinder, the sphere and the cone.

title: Gauguin's imagined color
description: In Vision of the Sermon (1888) Gauguin used flat, unnatural color, a red field, to show a vision in the praying women's imagination rather than a real scene.

facts.text: Gauguin's Vision of the Sermon (1888) is split by a tree: praying Breton women in white bonnets on one side, Jacob wrestling an angel on a red field on the other.
Gauguin wrote that the landscape and the fight exist only in the imagination of the people praying after the sermon.
Gauguin used pure, flat color and heavy outlines, and rejected painting straight from nature.

title: The Starry Night
description: Van Gogh, who painted some 900 paintings in about ten years and sold little, painted The Starry Night in 1889 at the Saint-Rémy asylum, from memory of the view from his barred window.

facts.text: In a career of about ten years, from 1880 to 1890, Van Gogh made some 900 paintings and 1,100 drawings.
Van Gogh sold little of his art while he was alive.
Van Gogh painted The Starry Night in 1889 at the asylum near Saint-Rémy, in southern France, from memory or drawings, as he couldn't paint in his bedroom.
The Starry Night shows swirling blue sky, a yellow crescent moon, stars as radiating orbs, a flame-like cypress at left and a village with glowing yellow windows.

title: Van Gogh's impasto
description: Van Gogh laid paint on thickly, squeezing it straight from the tube, so his strokes stand up from the canvas as impasto.

facts.text: For The Starry Night, Van Gogh applied paint straight from the tube onto the canvas, building thick impasto: paint laid on so thickly it stands up.

title: Van Gogh's color for feeling
description: Van Gogh used color to express emotion, as in The Night Café (1888), where he set red against green to express 'the terrible human passions'.

facts.text: In 1888, Van Gogh wrote to his brother Theo that in The Night Café he'd tried to express the terrible human passions with the red and the green.
Van Gogh described The Night Café's room as blood-red, with a green billiard table: everywhere a battle of greens and reds.

title: A Sunday on La Grande Jatte
description: Seurat's huge La Grande Jatte (1884–86), about 2 by 3 meters and two years in the making, shows Parisians relaxing on an island in the Seine, built from small strokes of color.

facts.text: Seurat's A Sunday on La Grande Jatte (1884–86), about 208 by 308 cm (about 2 by 3 meters), took him about two years.
La Grande Jatte shows Parisians strolling and picnicking on a Sunday afternoon on the Grande Jatte, an island in the Seine.

title: Pointillism: mixing in the eye
description: Seurat placed small dots of pure, unmixed color side by side so they blend in the viewer's eye from a distance, a method he called chromo-luminarism, now known as pointillism.

facts.text: Pointillism places small dots or strokes of color on a surface so that, from a distance, they blend together visually.
Seurat used tiny, separate strokes of pure color, too small to pick out when you view the whole work, which make his paintings shimmer.
Seurat met the chemist Michel-Eugène Chevreul, then about 100 years old, and experimented with Chevreul's theories of color.
Seurat called his method chromo-luminarism; it is also known as pointillism or divisionism.

title: Art Nouveau's line
description: Art Nouveau (about 1890–1910) was a deliberate new style of undulating, asymmetrical, plant-like lines, found mostly in architecture, interiors, jewelry, glass, posters and illustration.

facts.text: Art Nouveau flourished about 1890 to 1910 in Europe and the US; its undulating, asymmetrical line recalls flower stalks, vine tendrils and insect wings.
At its most energetic, the Art Nouveau line takes on a rhythmic, whiplike force.
Art Nouveau appeared most often in architecture, interior design, jewelry and glass design, posters and illustration.
Art Nouveau artists included the American glassmaker Louis Comfort Tiffany and the Czech designer Alphonse Mucha.
Art Nouveau was a deliberate attempt at a new style, free of the imitation of past styles that dominated much of 19th-century art.
Siegfried Bing's Paris gallery, L'Art Nouveau ("new art"), helped give the style its name.

title: Guimard's Métro entrances
description: From 1900, Hector Guimard's cast-iron Paris Métro entrances turned plant forms into street furniture; 86 of 141 survive, many lost when the style fell out of fashion.

facts.text: From 1900, Hector Guimard designed Paris Métro entrances in cast iron and glass, with plant-like ironwork, flower-bud lamps, green paint and a Métropolitain sign.
Only 86 of Guimard's 141 Métro entrances remain; many were demolished before Art Nouveau was appreciated again.
Parisians at first scorned Guimard's entrances and called the lettering on his signs un-French.
After 1910, Art Nouveau looked old-fashioned and was generally abandoned as a distinct style.

title: Munch's The Scream
description: Munch's The Scream (1893) grew from his account of sensing 'an infinite scream passing through nature' at sunset; its figure covers its ears under a blood-red sky.

facts.text: Munch's The Scream (1893) shows a figure with wide eyes, an oval open mouth and hands over its ears, under a swirling blood-red sky above the Oslo fjord.
Munch wrote that at sunset the sky turned blood red, and he stood trembling with anxiety and sensed an infinite scream passing through nature.

title: Expressionism
description: Expressionism shows the emotions things arouse in a person rather than how they objectively look, through distortion and exaggeration; Van Gogh, Munch and Ensor paved the way, and Die Brücke formed in Dresden in 1905.

facts.text: Expressionism depicts the emotions that objects and events arouse in a person rather than objective reality, using distortion and exaggeration.
Van Gogh, Munch and James Ensor paved the way for Expressionism, breaking with a literal copy of nature to express states of mind.
Die Brücke ("The Bridge"), an Expressionist group led by Ernst Ludwig Kirchner, formed in Dresden in 1905.
German Expressionists used jagged, distorted lines, rough, rapid brushwork and jarring colors to convey feelings such as anxiety.

title: Cubism's many views
description: Cubism showed several views of an object at once, broken into overlapping planes, and threw out traditional perspective and shading.

facts.text: Cubism showed several views of an object at once, broken into overlapping planes, rejecting traditional perspective and modeling and stressing the flat picture surface.

title: Picasso, Braque and Cubism
description: Picasso and Braque created Cubism in Paris between 1907 and 1914; a critic's 1908 jibe about 'cubes' named it, Cézanne inspired it, and after 1912 it added collage.

facts.text: Cubism, one of the 20th century's most influential styles, was created mainly by Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque in Paris between 1907 and 1914.
The critic Louis Vauxcelles mockingly described Braque's 1908 painting Houses at L'Estaque as made of cubes, which gave Cubism its name.
Cézanne's landscapes deeply inspired the Cubists in their first stage.
In Analytic Cubism (about 1910 to 1912), forms were broken down, in muted colors like tan, brown, gray and cream, often showing instruments, bottles, glasses and faces.
After 1912, in Synthetic Cubism, artists pasted materials such as newspaper and tobacco wrappers onto the canvas beside painted areas: collage.

title: Kandinsky's abstraction
description: Kandinsky saw one of his paintings on its side at dusk and decided objects harmed his paintings; he wanted color, line and shape to work like music.

facts.text: Kandinsky wrote in Reminiscences (1913) that at dusk he saw a glowing picture of forms and colors, then realized it was his own painting, standing on its side.
From that moment, Kandinsky wrote, he knew for certain that "the object harmed my paintings".
Kandinsky wanted colors, lines and shapes, freed from depicting objects, to form a visual language that, like music, could stir deep emotions.
Kandinsky's claim to be first rests mainly on a watercolor of color patches and black lines dated 1910; experts now think it was made in 1913.

title: Mondrian's grid
description: Mondrian's mature paintings use only straight horizontal and vertical lines, the primary colors and black, white and gray; he cofounded De Stijl in 1917.

facts.text: Mondrian's mature paintings use only straight horizontal and vertical lines, the primary colors, and black, white and gray.
In 1917 Mondrian cofounded De Stijl, a movement that restricted art to the most basic elements.

title: Hilma af Klint
description: Hilma af Klint painted abstract works in Stockholm from as early as 1906, before Kandinsky, but asked that they stay unseen until at least 20 years after her death in 1944.

facts.text: Art history textbooks long dated the birth of abstract painting to about 1910 to 1913 and credited Wassily Kandinsky.
Hilma af Klint was painting abstract works in her Stockholm studio as early as 1906.
Hilma af Klint asked that at least 20 years pass after her death before her work was shown; she died in 1944.

title: Dada
description: Dada began in 1916 at Hugo Ball's Cabaret Voltaire in Zurich, out of disgust with middle-class values and despair over World War I; its name, dada, is French for 'hobby-horse'.

facts.text: Dada began in Zurich in 1916 at Hugo Ball's Cabaret Voltaire, out of disgust for bourgeois values and despair over World War I.
Dada artists distrusted rational thought, believing it had led to violence and war.
By the widely told account, a paper knife stuck into a French-German dictionary chose the name: dada, French for "hobby-horse".

title: Duchamp's Fountain and the readymade
description: In 1917 Duchamp submitted Fountain, a porcelain urinal signed R. Mutt; as a readymade, it became art by the artist's choice, and in 2004 experts voted it the most influential modern artwork.

facts.text: Marcel Duchamp's Fountain (1917) is a white porcelain urinal, signed with a false name: R. Mutt.
Duchamp submitted Fountain to the 1917 exhibition of the Society of Independent Artists in New York, which took entries for a fee; though he was a founding member, it was refused.
Duchamp coined the word readymade for artworks made from manufactured objects he chose; his first was Bicycle Wheel (1913), a bicycle wheel mounted on a stool.
A 1917 editorial defended Fountain: "He CHOSE it," taking an ordinary article and placing it so its useful meaning disappeared under a new title.
The original Fountain was lost; it is known from Alfred Stieglitz's 1917 photograph, and museums show later replicas.
In 2004 a poll of 500 artists, curators, critics and dealers voted Fountain the most influential modern artwork, ahead of Picasso's Les Demoiselles d'Avignon.

title: Surrealism and the unconscious
description: André Breton's 1924 manifesto launched Surrealism, which grew out of Dada and, drawing on Freud, sought art in the unconscious and in dreams.

facts.text: The poet André Breton published the Manifesto of Surrealism in 1924.
Drawing on Freud, Breton saw the unconscious as the wellspring of imagination and wanted dream and fantasy joined to everyday reality.
Surrealism grew mainly out of Dada, but aimed at positive expression rather than Dada's negation.
Some Surrealists used automatic drawing, recording images spontaneously without censoring them.

title: Dalí's melting watches
description: Dalí's small painting The Persistence of Memory (1931) shows soft, melting pocket watches on the Catalan coast, painted realistically so the impossible looks real.

facts.text: Dalí said the soft watches in The Persistence of Memory were inspired by Camembert cheese.
Dalí's The Persistence of Memory (1931) is small, 24 by 33 cm, and shows melting watches, one over a ledge, and a distorted face on the coast of Catalonia, Dalí's home.
Surrealists such as Magritte and Dalí painted realistic images and removed them from their normal contexts.
Dalí declared that he did not know the meaning of The Persistence of Memory himself.

title: Magritte's pipe
description: Magritte's The Treachery of Images (1929) shows a pipe over the words 'This is not a pipe': a picture of a pipe is not a pipe.

facts.text: René Magritte's The Treachery of Images (1929) shows a plain pipe above the French words Ceci n'est pas une pipe ("This is not a pipe").
Magritte explained that nobody could smoke or fill the pipe in his picture, so it was not a pipe but a picture of one.

title: The 1913 Armory Show
description: The 1913 Armory Show brought European modern art to American crowds in New York, Chicago and Boston; it was mocked and even hanged in effigy, yet about 300,000 people saw it.

facts.text: The Armory Show ran from February 17 to March 15, 1913, at the 69th Regiment Armory in New York; about a third of its 1,600 works were European.
The Armory Show gave Americans a history of European modern art, including Impressionists, Post-Impressionists and Cubists.
Duchamp's Cubist painting Nude Descending a Staircase, No. 2 was popularly described as "an explosion in a shingle factory".
In Chicago, art students hanged Henri Matisse, Constantin Brancusi and Walter Pach in effigy.
The show traveled to New York, Chicago and Boston and was seen by about 300,000 Americans.
The Armory Show pushed American artists such as Georgia O'Keeffe and Stuart Davis toward avant-garde directions.

title: Ukiyo-e woodblock prints
description: Ukiyo-e, "pictures of the floating world", were Edo-period Japanese prints of actors, courtesans and landscapes, made cheaply by a team of publisher, artist, carver and printer, with a block per color.

facts.text: Ukiyo-e means "pictures of the floating world"; the floating world was the theater and pleasure districts of Japanese cities in the Edo period (1615–1868).
Ukiyo-e prints showed kabuki actors and courtesans, the style icons of their day, and later landscapes sold as travel souvenirs.
Woodblock printing let ukiyo-e prints be made cheaply and in large numbers, so they sold at a relatively low cost.
Each ukiyo-e print was a team effort: a publisher organized and sold it, an artist designed it in ink, a carver cut the blocks and a printer printed it.
The artist's final drawing was pasted face down on a block of cherry wood and carved through, which usually destroyed it; each color then needed its own carved block.
Registration marks called kento, carved on every block, kept the colors lined up; the printer inked each block and rubbed the paper onto it with a flat pad called a baren.

title: Hokusai's Great Wave
description: Hokusai's Under the Wave off Kanagawa (about 1830–32), from Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji: a claw-like wave over three boats, with Fuji small in its hollow.

facts.text: Hokusai's Under the Wave off Kanagawa, known as the Great Wave, comes from his print series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji and was made about 1830–32.
In the Great Wave, a huge wave with claw-like foam curls over three boats of rowers, while Mount Fuji, Japan's highest mountain, sits small in the hollow beneath it.
Hokusai (1760–1849) was about 70 when he designed the Great Wave.

title: Japonisme
description: After Japan reopened to Western trade in the 1850s, Japanese prints flooded Europe; the craze, named Japonisme in the early 1870s, taught artists flat color, bold stylization and asymmetric framing.

facts.text: From the 1630s Japan shut out the West, apart from a few Dutch traders at Nagasaki; wider trade resumed in the 1850s, and Japanese prints reached Europe.
Japonisme, the craze for Japanese art and design that swept France and the West, got its name in the early 1870s; the French critic Philippe Burty is generally said to have coined it.
Western artists admired Japanese prints for their flat areas of bright color, bold stylization, everyday subjects, asymmetrical compositions and unusual framing.

title: Monet, Degas and Van Gogh borrow from Japan
description: Monet hung over 200 Japanese prints at Giverny and built a print-like bridge; Degas borrowed asymmetry and framing; Van Gogh copied a Hiroshige print in 1887.

facts.text: Monet collected more than 200 Japanese prints, by Hokusai, Hiroshige, Utamaro and others, and hung them on the walls of his house at Giverny.
The bridge over Monet's water garden at Giverny recalls the Japanese bridges often shown in Japanese prints.
Degas collected Japanese prints and borrowed their asymmetrical compositions and framing devices, such as a doorframe cutting into the side of a scene.
In 1887 Van Gogh painted Bridge in the Rain after a Hiroshige print, making the colors more intense and filling its border with Japanese characters copied from other prints.

title: Calligraphy as China's highest art
description: Chinese calligraphy (shufa) has been ranked supreme among China's visual arts since the 3rd century CE; it uses the Four Treasures, allows no touching up and is thought to reveal the writer's character.

facts.text: Since the 3rd century CE, calligraphy (shufa, writing as a fine art) has been considered supreme among the visual arts in China, above painting.
Brush, ink, paper and inkstone, the calligrapher's tools, are honored as the Four Treasures of the Study.
A calligraphy stroke cannot be touched up: once the ink dries, a corrected area shows darker than the original stroke.
Chinese calligraphy is regarded as uniquely revealing the character and cultivation of the writer.
Chinese painters use the same brush and ink as calligraphers, and both arts are judged by similar standards, above all the vitality of the brushstroke.

title: Wang Xizhi's Orchid Pavilion Preface
description: Wang Xizhi, the Sage of Calligraphy, wrote the Preface to the Orchid Pavilion in 353; legend says the original was buried with Emperor Taizong, so it survives only in copies.

facts.text: Wang Xizhi (303–361) is traditionally called the Sage of Calligraphy and is often considered the greatest Chinese calligrapher of all time.
Wang Xizhi wrote the Preface to the Orchid Pavilion in 353; the story goes that he wrote it tipsy, then tried a thousand times to rewrite it and never matched it.
According to legend, the Tang emperor Taizong loved the original Orchid Pavilion Preface so much that it was buried with him; today it is known only through copies.

title: The Benin Bronzes
description: Court art of the Kingdom of Benin (Edo State, Nigeria): brass plaques for the oba's palace pillars and heads for royal ancestral altars, cast by lost wax by the Igun Eronmwon guild, which still works today.

facts.text: The Kingdom of Benin, in what is now Edo State, Nigeria (not the modern Republic of Benin), flourished from the 13th to the 19th century under its oba, or king.
Benin's brass casters belonged to a royal guild, Igun Eronmwon, the highest-ranking of the palace guilds, and cast their works by the lost-wax method.
In lost-wax casting, a wax model (often built over a clay core) is coated in clay and heated so the wax runs out; molten metal is then poured into the space.
Brass casters of the Igun Eronmwon guild still work on Igun Street in Benin City today.
Despite their name, the Benin Bronzes are mostly brass, and the group also includes works of ivory, wood and other materials.
Brass relief plaques, arranged to tell the court's story, were nailed onto the pillars of the oba's palace, and brass heads on royal ancestral altars held up carved ivory tusks.

title: The 1897 looting and the return debate
description: British forces looted thousands of works from Benin City in 1897; in 2022 Germany and the Smithsonian transferred ownership of Benin Bronzes to Nigeria, while other museums still hold large collections.

facts.text: In 1897 a British force invaded Benin City, burned it and looted the royal palace, taking thousands of objects.
In 2022 Germany transferred ownership of more than 1,100 Benin Bronzes to Nigeria, and the Smithsonian transferred ownership of 29.
Many other museums, including the British Museum, still hold large collections of Benin Bronzes, and calls for their return continue.

title: Masks in masquerade
description: In many African traditions a mask is one part of a masquerade of costume, music and dance in which performers may embody spirits or ancestors, as in Yoruba Egungun.

facts.text: In many African traditions a mask is only one part of a masquerade: a performance with a full costume, music and dance.
Masqueraders may embody spirits or ancestors; audiences know a person is inside, yet accept that the spirit is present.
In Yoruba Egungun masquerades in Nigeria, a performer hidden under layers of fine cloth becomes a returned ancestor; when he spins, the cloth panels flare open.

title: African sculpture and modern art
description: Matisse, Derain and Vlaminck collected African sculpture; after studying masks at the Trocadéro in 1907, Picasso gave figures in Les Demoiselles d'Avignon mask-like faces.

facts.text: In fall 1906 Matisse bought a small Vili figure from Central Africa in a Paris curio shop and showed it to Picasso.
Matisse, Derain and Vlaminck were early collectors of African sculpture in Paris.
In 1907 Picasso studied African masks and sculpture at the Trocadéro ethnographic museum in Paris.
After studying African masks in 1907, Picasso repainted faces in his painting Les Demoiselles d'Avignon so they looked like masks.

title: The makers behind the objects
description: African works reached Paris largely through colonial collecting and were labeled by people, not artist; named masters like Olowe of Ise were famous in their own lifetimes.

facts.text: Many of the Trocadéro's African objects flowed in from France's colonies, crowding the museum like a giant curiosity cabinet.
Western collectors and museums usually grouped African works by people or "tribe" rather than naming the artist, and modernists responded mainly to their forms, not their meanings.
Olowe of Ise (about 1873–1938), a Yoruba sculptor active in the early 1900s, was sought out by Yoruba kings to carve palace doors and veranda posts.
In 1924 a door Olowe of Ise carved for the king's palace at Ikere was shown at the British Empire Exhibition in London, and the British Museum later acquired it.

title: Ancient Aboriginal rock art
description: A kangaroo painted on a Kimberley rock-shelter ceiling about 17,300 years ago is Australia's oldest known intact rock painting, dated from wasp nests beneath and on top of the paint.

facts.text: A 2-metre kangaroo painted on a rock-shelter ceiling on Balanggarra Country in the Kimberley is about 17,300 years old, Australia's oldest known intact rock painting.
Researchers radiocarbon-dated mud wasp nests: nests beneath the paint give a maximum age for the kangaroo, and nests built on top of it give a minimum age.
The Kimberley dating was carried out with the permission and involvement of Traditional Owners.

title: Papunya and Western Desert dot painting
description: Paintings of Jukurrpa (the Dreaming); the 1971 Honey Ant Dreaming mural at Papunya began the Western Desert movement, where dots came to veil sacred designs; dots are a Western Desert style, not all Aboriginal art.

facts.text: In Warlpiri, Jukurrpa, often translated as the Dreaming, is the creation era when ancestral beings shaped the land and laid down the law; many desert paintings depict it.
In 1971 at Papunya, in the Northern Territory, Aboriginal men led by Kaapa Tjampitjinpa painted a Honey Ant Dreaming mural on the school wall, encouraged by teacher Geoffrey Bardon.
After the mural, men at Papunya began painting their ancestral stories on boards and other surfaces, the start of the Western Desert painting movement.
In 1972 the Papunya painters formed their own company, Papunya Tula Artists.
As Western Desert paintings reached wider audiences, artists increasingly used dots to cover secret and sacred designs.
Dot painting comes from the Western Desert around Papunya; many other Aboriginal nations have their own, different visual languages, and some artists object to dots standing in for everyone.

title: Maya stelae
description: Classic Maya stelae are free-standing carved stone slabs with rulers' portraits and hieroglyphic texts naming them and recording dates and deeds; Copán's are famous.

facts.text: Classic Maya stelae are free-standing stone slabs carved in relief, usually with a ruler's portrait and hieroglyphic texts naming the ruler and recording dates and deeds.
Copán, in today's Honduras, is famous for its massive, highly detailed figurative stelae.

title: The Mexica Sun Stone
description: The basalt Sun Stone, probably carved 1502–1521, found buried in Mexico City in 1790: its central face is debated, it shows the current era 4 Movement, and despite its nickname it cannot tell the date.

facts.text: The Sun Stone of the Mexica, the people often called the Aztecs, is a basalt disc about 3.6 meters across, probably carved between 1502 and 1521.
In December 1790 the Sun Stone was found buried face down in Mexico City's main plaza, built over the heart of the Mexica capital, Tenochtitlan.
The face at the center of the Sun Stone is traditionally identified as the sun god Tonatiuh; some scholars argue it is the earth deity Tlaltecuhtli, or a blend of the two.
The Sun Stone shows the current world era, 4 Movement (Nahui Ollin), which the Mexica believed would end in earthquakes.
Although nicknamed the Calendar Stone, the Sun Stone shows its twenty day signs with no numbers attached, so it cannot tell the date; many scholars think it served as an altar.
Soon after its discovery, the scholar Antonio de León y Gama read the Sun Stone as a timekeeping device, and that view dominated for about a century.

title: Inca stonework and cloth
description: Inca builders fitted stones without mortar so tightly a knife blade cannot slip between them, walls that survived Cusco's 1650 earthquake; the finest cloth, qompi, was prized above gold.

facts.text: Inca builders fitted stones without mortar, so precisely that even a thin knife blade cannot slip between them.
When an earthquake struck Cusco in 1650, most Spanish colonial buildings crumbled, but Inca walls and foundations survived nearly intact.
For the Inca, the finest cloth, called qompi, was among the most prized possessions, more precious than gold or silver.

title: Mexican muralism
description: From 1921 education minister José Vasconcelos commissioned murals on public buildings to teach history to a largely illiterate population; led by los tres grandes, Rivera, Orozco and Siqueiros.

facts.text: After the Mexican Revolution, from 1921, education minister José Vasconcelos commissioned murals on public buildings to teach Mexico's history to a largely illiterate population.
Diego Rivera, José Clemente Orozco and David Alfaro Siqueiros, the leaders of Mexican muralism, were known as los tres grandes, the Three Great Ones.
In Europe Rivera painted in a Cubist style alongside friends such as Picasso and Braque, and studied frescoes in Italy before returning to Mexico in 1921.
Wall paintings appealed to Rivera because anyone could see them, including people who could not visit galleries or museums.

title: Rivera's murals
description: Rivera's fresco The History of Mexico (1929–35) in the National Palace stairwell, and his 1933 Rockefeller Center mural, destroyed in 1934 after he refused to remove Lenin.

facts.text: In true fresco, pigments are painted onto fresh, wet lime plaster and become part of the wall as it dries.
Between 1929 and 1935 Rivera painted The History of Mexico across three walls of the National Palace stairwell in Mexico City, from ancient Mexico through the Spanish conquest to an imagined future.
The mural's ancient section shows the Valley of Mexico with a pyramid and scenes of life before the conquest, such as people grinding maize and making art.

In 1933 Rivera's mural for Rockefeller Center in New York included a portrait of Lenin; Nelson Rockefeller objected, Rivera refused to remove it, and the unfinished mural was covered and destroyed in 1934.
Rivera repainted the Rockefeller Center design as Man, Controller of the Universe at the Palace of Fine Arts in Mexico City.

title: Kahlo's self-portraits
description: Injured in a 1925 bus accident at 18, Kahlo taught herself to paint in bed from a mirror; she painted 55 self-portraits exploring identity, the body and death.

facts.text: In 1925, at 18, Frida Kahlo was badly injured in a bus accident, with multiple fractures including her spine, and spent months in plaster casts.
While recovering in bed, Kahlo taught herself to paint, painting her own image from a mirror attached to her bed's canopy.
Frida Kahlo painted 55 self-portraits.
Kahlo said she painted herself because she was so often alone and was the subject she knew best.
Kahlo's brilliantly colored self-portraits deal with themes such as identity, the human body and death.

title: Symbols in Kahlo's paintings
description: The Two Fridas (1939) pairs European and Tehuana selves joined by an artery; the 1940 thorn-necklace self-portrait uses thorns, a dead hummingbird, a cat and a monkey, symbols read in several ways.

facts.text: Kahlo often wore traditional Tehuana dress and drew on Mexican folk art.
The Two Fridas (1939) shows two Kahlos side by side, one in a white European-style dress and one in Tehuana dress, their exposed hearts joined by an artery.
In The Two Fridas, the European-dressed Frida has cut the artery with scissors and blood stains her skirt; the Tehuana Frida holds a small portrait of Diego Rivera.
Kahlo painted The Two Fridas in 1939, after separating from Diego Rivera, whom she had married in 1929.
The two dresses in The Two Fridas are often read as Kahlo's European and Mexican heritage.
In Self-Portrait with Thorn Necklace and Hummingbird (1940), a necklace of thorns digs into her neck with a dead hummingbird hanging from it, and a black cat and a monkey appear behind her shoulders.
Scholars read the 1940 self-portrait's symbols in many ways: the thorns can recall Christ's crown of thorns, and dead hummingbirds were Mexican folk charms for luck in love.
Often called a Surrealist, Kahlo distanced herself from the label, saying she painted her own reality, not dreams.

title: Prussian blue: influence both ways
description: Prussian blue, invented in Berlin around 1705, reached Japan as bero and colored Hokusai's Fuji series; Europeans then admired it as a Japanese blue. Influence runs in both directions.

facts.text: Prussian blue, the first modern synthetic pigment, was created by accident in Berlin around 1705.
By the early 1800s Prussian blue was being made more cheaply in China, and it reached Japan, where it was called bero, from the Dutch for "Berlin blue".
Hokusai used Prussian blue extensively in Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, including the Great Wave.
Europeans admiring Japanese prints often took their vivid blue for a traditional Japanese color, though it was a European invention.

title: Pollock and action painting
description: Abstract Expressionism began in New York in the late 1940s. Pollock poured and dripped paint on canvas laid on the floor, and critics called the canvas an arena in which to act.

facts.text: Pollock painted Autumn Rhythm (Number 30) in July and August 1950 on unstretched canvas laid flat on his studio floor; it is about 17 feet wide and 8 feet high.
Pollock poured, dripped and flicked thinned paint, working around the canvas from all sides with sticks, trowels and knives, and built up dense webs of line.
The critic Harold Rosenberg called these painters "action painters" because, to him, the canvas had become an arena in which to act.
Abstract Expressionism began in New York in the late 1940s and shifted the creative center of modern painting from Paris to New York.

title: Rothko and color-field painting
description: Rothko painted soft-edged rectangles of color on wall-sized canvases to express basic human emotions, and made dark paintings for a chapel in Houston.

facts.text: Rothko's mature paintings show two or three soft-edged rectangles of color that nearly fill wall-sized vertical canvases.
Color-field painters like Rothko used large fields of flat color and thin paint to achieve quiet, almost meditative effects.
Rothko said his paintings expressed basic human emotions, such as tragedy, ecstasy and doom.
In 1964 the de Menils commissioned Rothko to paint dark works in browns, maroons and blacks for a nondenominational chapel in Houston; it opened in 1971, after Rothko died in 1970.

title: Pop Art's sources
description: Pop Art, from the 1950s in Britain and America, took its images from ads, packaging, films and comics, and turned away from Abstract Expressionism's personal feelings.

facts.text: Richard Hamilton's 1956 collage for London's This Is Tomorrow exhibition, made from American magazine images, shows a bodybuilder holding a giant lollipop labeled POP in a crowded living room.
Pop art emerged in the 1950s and flourished in the 1960s in Britain and America, taking its imagery from Hollywood movies, advertising, product packaging, pop music and comic books.
In 1957 Richard Hamilton listed what Pop art should be, including popular, expendable, low cost, mass produced, witty and big business.
By using impersonal, everyday imagery, Pop artists moved away from the personal feelings and symbolism at the heart of Abstract Expressionism.

title: Lichtenstein's comic paintings
description: Roy Lichtenstein painted single comic panels, imitating cheap printing with black outlines, primary colors and Benday dots, as in Whaam! (1963).

facts.text: Lichtenstein's Whaam! (1963) is based on a panel from a 1962 DC war comic, All-American Men of War; its two panels show the attacking plane on the left and the explosion on the right.
Lichtenstein outlined areas of primary color with thick black lines and imitated Benday dots, a dot pattern used in commercial printing.
Lichtenstein made the Benday dots in Whaam! by hand, using a scrub brush and a handmade metal screen.

title: Warhol's repeated images
description: Warhol repeated consumer goods and celebrities, from 32 soup cans to 50 Marilyns, using photographic silkscreen to print the same image again and again.

facts.text: Warhol's Campbell's Soup Cans (1962) is 32 canvases, one for each flavor then sold; at the Ferus Gallery in Los Angeles in 1962 they sat on narrow ledges like groceries on a shelf.
Before his Pop paintings, Warhol worked as a commercial illustrator in New York for about a decade.
Warhol mass-produced images with photographic silkscreen, a stencil printing process that can print the same image again and again.
Warhol made Marilyn Diptych (1962) in the weeks after Marilyn Monroe died in August 1962: one publicity photo repeated 50 times, 25 in color on the left and 25 in black and white on the right.

title: The Factory and the artist as machine
description: Warhol ran his studio, the Factory, like a production line and said in 1963 that he wanted to be a machine.

facts.text: From 1964 Warhol's New York studio, the Factory, was covered in silver foil and silver paint by his collaborator Billy Name.
The Factory drew underground film and rock music stars and assorted hangers-on.
In a 1963 ARTnews interview Warhol said he wanted to be a machine, and that somebody else should be able to do all his paintings for him; he tied this to using silkscreens.

title: Minimalism
description: Minimalism, from 1960s America, used simple geometric shapes, often industrially made, that refer to nothing but themselves.

facts.text: Minimalism is an extreme form of abstract art developed in the USA in the 1960s, made of simple geometric shapes based on the square and the rectangle.
Minimalists thought Action painting too personal and held that a work of art should not refer to anything other than itself.
In a 1964 interview, the painter Frank Stella summed up his work with the phrase "What you see is what you see."

Donald Judd had his works made by professional fabricators in industrial materials like galvanized iron and Plexiglas; his stacks, begun in 1965, are identical boxes hung one above another on a wall at equal intervals.

title: Carl Andre's bricks
description: Carl Andre's Equivalent VIII (1966), 120 firebricks bought by the Tate in 1972, set off a public row about Minimalism in 1976.

facts.text: Carl Andre's Equivalent VIII (1966) is 120 firebricks laid in two layers in a rectangle; the Tate bought it in 1972.
In 1976 newspaper coverage of the Tate's purchase set off a public furor, one of Britain's best-known rows about contemporary art.

title: LeWitt: the idea makes the art
description: In conceptual art the idea matters most; Sol LeWitt's wall drawings are instructions that other people carry out.

facts.text: Conceptual art is art in which the idea behind the work matters more than the finished object; it emerged as a movement in the 1960s.
In "Paragraphs on Conceptual Art" (1967), Sol LeWitt wrote that the idea is the most important aspect of the work, and that the idea becomes a machine that makes the art.
LeWitt's wall drawings begin as instructions, often with a diagram, that assistants carry out on the wall, so each version differs slightly.
A retrospective of LeWitt's wall drawings opened at MASS MoCA in 2008, the year after he died, drawn over nearly six months by assistants, students and local artists.

title: Kosuth's One and Three Chairs
description: Joseph Kosuth's One and Three Chairs (1965) shows a chair as an object, a photo and a dictionary definition.

facts.text: Joseph Kosuth's One and Three Chairs (1965) combines a wooden folding chair, a photograph of a chair and an enlarged dictionary definition of the word chair.
Kosuth did not make the chair, take the photograph or write the definition; he selected and arranged them.

title: From Pictorialism to straight photography
description: Early art photographers made photos look like paintings; in 1932 Group f/64 championed sharp, straight photography instead.

facts.text: The Photo-Secession, founded in 1902 with Alfred Stieglitz, promoted Pictorialism: manipulating negatives and prints to look like drawings, etchings and oil paintings.
Alfred Stieglitz championed photography as a fine art, equal to painting.

Group f/64, formed in San Francisco in 1932 by photographers including Ansel Adams and Edward Weston, championed "straight" photography; f/64 is a small lens opening that gives sharp focus and fine detail.

title: Ansel Adams and photography in the museum
description: Adams took Moonrise, Hernandez in 1941 and reprinted it for years with more contrast; in 1940 MoMA founded a department of photography with his help.

facts.text: Adams took Moonrise, Hernandez, New Mexico in 1941 without his light meter, working out the exposure from the moon's brightness; the light left the graveyard crosses before he could make a second negative.
Adams printed Moonrise many times over the years, increasing the contrast to make the moon whiter and the sky darker.
In 1940, working closely with Ansel Adams, Beaumont Newhall founded the Museum of Modern Art's department of photography.

title: Land art and Spiral Jetty
description: Land art is made in the landscape itself; Smithson's Spiral Jetty (1970) is a rock coil in Great Salt Lake that sinks and reappears with the water.

facts.text: Land art is made directly in the landscape, from earth or natural materials such as rocks; it was part of the wider conceptual art movement of the 1960s and 1970s.
In 1970 Robert Smithson built Spiral Jetty from about 6,000 tons of black basalt rock and earth: a coil 1,500 feet long winding counterclockwise into Utah's Great Salt Lake.

Spiral Jetty was built when the lake was low, was submerged in 1972, and has been visible since droughts lowered the lake in 2002, about 30 years later; it is made of mud, salt crystals, rocks and water.

title: Installation art and Kusama's mirror rooms
description: Installation art fills a whole room you walk into; Kusama's first Infinity Mirror Room (1965) used mirrors to make repeated forms seem endless.

facts.text: Installation art often fills a whole room or gallery that the viewer walks through, which makes it an immersive experience.
Kusama's first mirror room, Infinity Mirror Room: Phalli's Field (1965), filled a closed room with stuffed fabric forms covered in red polka dots, reflected seemingly endlessly by mirrored walls.

title: Street art moves indoors
description: Keith Haring drew in chalk in the subway and Basquiat wrote SAMO graffiti before both became gallery artists.

facts.text: From 1980 to 1985 Keith Haring made hundreds, if not thousands, of illegal chalk drawings on the black paper covering unrented subway ad panels, and was arrested many times.

In the late 1970s Jean-Michel Basquiat and Al Diaz spray-painted cryptic sayings signed SAMO on walls in Lower Manhattan; around 1980 Basquiat gave up SAMO to paint, and by the early 1980s his work was shown internationally.

title: Banksy
description: Banksy, an anonymous British street artist, works with stencils for speed; in 2018 his Girl with Balloon shredded itself just after it sold at auction.

facts.text: Banksy, an anonymous British graffiti artist, has used stencils since 2000 to work faster, building up images such as rats and policemen.
In 2018 Banksy's Girl with Balloon partly shredded itself, through a shredder hidden in its frame, just after selling at Sotheby's for $1.4 million; it became a new work, Love Is in the Bin.

title: What makes a painting priceless
description: The Salvator Mundi went from a damaged auction find in 2005 to $450.3 million in 2017, mainly because it was attributed to Leonardo, a disputed attribution.

facts.text: In 2005 two dealers bought the Salvator Mundi, a painting of Christ, at a small auction in New Orleans; it was in bad shape and heavily overpainted.
On 15 November 2017 the Salvator Mundi sold at Christie's in New York for $450.3 million, a record for any painting sold at auction.
After cleaning and study, the Salvator Mundi was authenticated as a Leonardo by 2011; Christie's called it one of fewer than 20 known paintings by him.
The attribution is not universally accepted: some specialists think Leonardo painted only parts of it, and others say heavy restoration makes a firm verdict impossible.

title: How auctions set record prices
description: At auction a price climbs only while rivals keep bidding; the Salvator Mundi sale came down to two bidders, and fame can set records too.

facts.text: The Salvator Mundi bidding lasted about 19 minutes and came down to two bidders on the phone; the winning bid was $400 million, and fees brought the price to $450.3 million.
Warhol's Shot Sage Blue Marilyn (1964), a silkscreen portrait of Monroe, sold at Christie's New York in May 2022 for $195 million, then the highest auction price for a 20th-century artwork.

title: The dematerialization of art
description: From the late 1940s on, art moved from paint on canvas toward ideas and instructions; in 1968 critics called this the dematerialization of art.

facts.text: In 1968 Lucy Lippard and John Chandler's essay "The Dematerialization of Art" described "ultra-conceptual" art in which the idea matters more than the object.

title: Slow looking
description: Museum visitors spend on average only about 27 seconds with each artwork; close looking takes longer.

facts.text: A 2001 study that unobtrusively timed visitors at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York found they looked at each artwork for 27.2 seconds on average, about 27 seconds.

title: Landscape with the Fall of Icarus
description: In the Icarus painting credited to Bruegel, Icarus is only a pair of legs in the sea while ordinary life goes on; it rewards slow looking and invites several readings.

facts.text: In Greek myth, Icarus flew on wings of feathers and wax made by his father Daedalus, went too near the Sun, and fell into the sea and drowned.
In Landscape with the Fall of Icarus, a farmer ploughs, a shepherd daydreams and a ship passes; Icarus is only a pair of legs in the sea near the ship, lower right, easily missed at a casual glance.
The Brussels Landscape with the Fall of Icarus dates to about 1560; many scholars think it is an early copy, made in the 1560s, of a lost Bruegel original of about 1558.
One common reading of the Icarus painting is that ordinary life carries on unmoved while Icarus drowns; Britannica also reads a moral that pride and ambition lead to a fall.

title: Feldman's four steps
description: Edmund Burke Feldman's method for looking at art: describe, analyze, interpret, then judge, with judgment held to the end.

facts.text: Art educator Edmund Burke Feldman's method has four steps: describe what you see (including line, shape, color and texture), analyze how the parts work together and where the focus is, interpret meaning, and judge.
In Feldman's method the steps are taken in order: judgment and opinion wait until the end, and careful description is the basis for every other step.

title: Balance
description: Balance is the spread of visual weight in a picture: symmetrical, asymmetrical or radial.

facts.text: Balance is the distribution of visual weight; like a scale, balanced weight makes a design feel stable. Symmetrical: sides alike; asymmetrical: sides differ but still look balanced; radial: arranged around a central point.

title: Emphasis and movement
description: Emphasis creates a focal point by contrast; movement is the path the eye takes, as along the diagonal in Bruegel's Hunters in the Snow.

facts.text: Emphasis is the part of a design that catches the viewer's attention first, the focal point; artists usually make it stand out by contrast in size, color, texture or shape.
Movement is the path the viewer's eye takes through a work of art, often to focal areas, directed along lines, edges, shapes and colors.
Bruegel's Hunters in the Snow (1565), in Vienna, shows hunters returning with tired dogs and a single fox, above frozen ponds full of skaters.
In Hunters in the Snow, a diagonal arrangement, including a line of bare trees, leads the viewer's eye from the hunters down into the distant landscape.

title: The rule of thirds
description: The rule of thirds, named by John Thomas Smith in 1797, places key elements on the lines of a 3 by 3 grid rather than dead center.

facts.text: The phrase 'rule of thirds' was first written down by John Thomas Smith in 1797 in Remarks on Rural Scenery, a book for landscape painters; he offered it as a rule of thumb.
The rule of thirds divides an image into nine equal parts with two horizontal and two vertical lines and places key elements along those lines or where they cross.

title: Skulls and memento mori
description: A skull is a memento mori, a reminder of death; vanitas still lifes add symbols of passing pleasures; Holbein hid one in The Ambassadors.

facts.text: In Holbein's The Ambassadors (1533), a distorted shape between the two men's feet becomes a large skull when seen from the painting's bottom right corner, an effect called anamorphosis.
Memento mori is Latin for 'remember you must die'; memento mori artworks remind viewers of mortality, and the skull is the classic symbol.

A vanitas still life uses symbols such as a skull, an extinguished candle, musical instruments, wine and books to warn of mortality and the worthlessness of worldly pleasures; such pictures became popular in the 1600s, a religious age.

title: Lilies and dogs
description: White lilies stand for purity and the Virgin Mary; dogs can stand for faithfulness; symbols are clues to interpret, not a fixed code.

facts.text: White lilies are generally thought to represent purity, linking them to the Virgin Mary; in Annunciation scenes Gabriel holds one or it stands in a vase. Lilies also belong to saints such as Catherine of Siena.
In Jan van Eyck's Arnolfini Portrait (1434), a small dog with every hair painted stands at the couple's feet; dogs were a common sign of faithfulness in marriage.
The National Gallery's glossary says the Arnolfini dog 'may be intended' to symbolize the couple's fidelity.

title: How public museums began
description: From the Tradescants' Ark (1634) to the Ashmolean (1683), the British Museum (1753) and the public Louvre (1793).

facts.text: The Louvre in Paris began as a royal residence, begun by Francis I in 1546; in 1793 France's revolutionary government opened its Grande Galerie to the public as a museum.

In 1634 the gardeners John Tradescant and his son opened a museum, the Ark, in their Lambeth home in south London; a visitor said one could see more curiosities there in a day than in a lifetime of travel. It held a preserved dodo.
Elias Ashmole acquired the Tradescant collection and gave it to Oxford University; the Ashmolean opened in 1683 as Britain's first public museum.
The British Museum was founded by Act of Parliament in 1753, for 'all studious and curious persons', and opened free to the public in 1759.

title: What museums do today
description: ICOM's 2022 definition: a museum researches, collects, conserves, interprets and exhibits heritage for society.

facts.text: In 2022 the International Council of Museums approved a definition: a museum is a not-for-profit, permanent institution in the service of society that researches, collects, conserves, interprets and exhibits heritage.

title: Reversible conservation
description: Modern conservators make every treatment reversible; Borja's 2012 amateur touch-up shows what happens without training.

facts.text: In 2012, Cecilia Giménez, an amateur painter in her eighties, tried to restore the Ecce Homo fresco of Christ in her church in Borja, Spain; the head came to look like a hairy monkey, and 'Monkey Christ' went viral.
The church foundation in Borja said Giménez acted with the best intentions.
London's National Gallery fills and retouches losses, and says that, unlike past restorations, all its work is reversible and/or removable should future generations need to remove it.

title: Cleaning varnish
description: Old varnish discolors into a yellowish fog; conservators remove it to reveal the colors underneath.

facts.text: Varnish discolors with age, giving a painting a yellowed, foggy look; conservators clean off dirt and old varnish to reveal the original colors.
A National Gallery conservator, Larry Keith, removed 75 years' worth of discolored varnish from Rubens's landscape 'Het Steen'.

title: The Ghent Lamb
description: Removing 16th-century overpaint from the Ghent Altarpiece in 2019 revealed the van Eycks' strikingly human-faced Lamb.

facts.text: The Ghent Altarpiece, finished by Jan and Hubert van Eyck by 1432, had its Lamb of God overpainted with a calmer, more animal face around 1550; in 2019 Belgium's Royal Institute for Cultural Heritage removed it with solvents and scalpels, revealing forward-gazing, strikingly human eyes.
The Lamb's revealed face was widely mocked online; a 2020 study in Science Advances found it matched the van Eycks' original.

title: Han van Meegeren's fake Vermeers
description: Van Meegeren sold a fake Vermeer to Göring, confessed in 1945 and proved it by painting another under watch.

facts.text: After World War II, a supposed painting by the 17th-century Dutch master Johannes Vermeer turned up in Hermann Göring's collection; Han van Meegeren, who sold it, was arrested in 1945 for collaboration and confessed he had painted it.
To prove his claim, van Meegeren painted another 'Vermeer' under observation by the authorities, using the same materials and techniques.

Van Meegeren scraped most of the picture off a real 17th-century painting, keeping its network of cracks, mixed his paint with the synthetic resin Bakelite, and baked the canvas so it set hard like old paint.
In 1947 van Meegeren was convicted of forgery and sentenced to one year in prison, but he died of a heart attack before serving it.

title: Materials betray forgers
description: Lab tests find materials that did not exist at a painting's supposed date: Bakelite and cobalt blue for van Meegeren, titanium white for Beltracchi.

facts.text: Tests by Paul Coremans, head of Belgium's central museum laboratory, found phenol-formaldehyde resin (Bakelite) in van Meegeren's paint, and cobalt blue, not made until the 1800s, in two paintings.
Bakelite, the first fully synthetic plastic, a phenol-formaldehyde resin, was invented by Leo Baekeland in 1907.

Wolfgang Beltracchi painted new works 'in the style of' artists such as Max Ernst and Heinrich Campendonk; titanium white, not yet in use in 1914, found in a supposed 1914 Campendonk exposed him, and in 2011 he was sentenced to six years.

title: The 1911 Mona Lisa theft
description: A former Louvre worker stole the Mona Lisa in 1911; the sensation made it world-famous before it was recovered in Florence in 1913.

facts.text: The Mona Lisa shows a woman with a mysterious smile set against a distant landscape.

On the morning of August 21, 1911, Vincenzo Peruggia, an Italian who had worked at the Louvre fitting glass on paintings, took the Mona Lisa after hiding in a closet overnight, and left without suspicion.
Because paintings were often taken down for cleaning, the theft went unnoticed for over a day; police questioned suspects including Pablo Picasso, who was cleared.
The 1911 theft became a media sensation: people flocked to the Louvre to see the empty space, and the coverage made the painting world-famous.
In 1913 Peruggia tried to sell the Mona Lisa to an art dealer in Florence, who alerted the authorities; it was found in the false bottom of his trunk.

title: The Gardner Museum theft
description: In 1990 thieves dressed as police stole 13 works from Boston's Gardner Museum; unsolved, with empty frames still hanging.

facts.text: In the early hours of March 18, 1990, two men in police uniforms got into Boston's Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum, restrained the guards and stole 13 works, including works by Rembrandt and Vermeer; the theft is unsolved.
The Gardner Museum offers a $10 million reward, and empty frames still hang where the stolen paintings were.
Famous stolen artworks are nearly impossible to sell openly because they are so recognizable.

title: The first computer art
description: Georg Nees showed computer-drawn graphics in Stuttgart in 1965; his Schotter uses randomness to turn order into chaos.

facts.text: In February 1965, Georg Nees, a mathematician working as a software engineer at Siemens, showed computer graphics drawn by a machine from his programs at the Technische Hochschule in Stuttgart, one of the first such exhibitions.
Nees's Schotter ('gravel'), printed from 1968 to 1970, shows rows of orderly squares that descend into chaos because Nees built random variables into his program, exploring order and disorder.

title: AARON
description: Harold Cohen's AARON, begun in 1973, was a program that made drawings on its own from rules he wrote.

facts.text: In 1973 the painter Harold Cohen began AARON, a program that made drawings on its own from rules he wrote; early on, a small robot 'turtle' holding a marker drew them.
For about 20 years Cohen colored AARON's drawings by hand; AARON colored on its own only from 1995.

title: NFT art
description: In 2021 Beeple's Everydays sold as an NFT, a blockchain token certifying ownership of a digital item, for $69.3 million.

facts.text: Beeple (Mike Winkelmann) made an image every day from 2007 and combined 5,000 into a collage, Everydays: The First 5000 Days, sold as an NFT at Christie's in March 2021 for $69.3 million, the first purely digital artwork sold as an NFT by a major auction house.
An NFT (non-fungible token) is a unique digital token, authenticated with blockchain technology, that certifies authenticity and ownership of a digital item.

title: New readings keep art alive
description: Art lasts when it survives, stays seen and keeps getting new readings, as Auden's and Williams's poems on the Icarus painting show.

facts.text: In the winter of 1938, W. H. Auden saw Bruegel's Landscape with the Fall of Icarus in Brussels and wrote the poem 'Musée des Beaux Arts', which reads it as suffering happening while ordinary life goes on.
William Carlos Williams wrote his own poem, 'Landscape with the Fall of Icarus', in the early 1960s; it ends 'a splash quite unnoticed / this was / Icarus drowning'.
